We propose new algorithms that align Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) graph constituents with sentences without requiring manual annotations or separate syntactic parsing. By combining unsupervised models—tuned to graph substructures—with heuristics, our approach merges advantages of prior aligners. Our system handles diverse and complex substructures previously unmanaged in methods that depended solely on parse information, resulting in broader node and edge coverage with superior accuracy. We plan to release the dedicated LEAMR aligner and accompanying datasets to advance research across AMR parsing, generation, and evaluation tasks.

Recent data-based single-view approaches have advanced our modeling of 3D dressed individuals, yet they face significant limitations due to depth uncertainties and the effects of occultation found in one-image inputs. This work addresses these challenges by leveraging an assembly of sparse input views and determining the most effective strategies for synthesizing data from them. We present a fully automated, data-driven framework that generates implicit 3D representations of clothed humans from minimal camera perspectives. Our methodology incorporates three primary elements: 1) a system for maintaining spatial consistency that enables arbitrary positioning of individuals within multi-perspective scenes; 2) an attention-driven fusion module designed to merge insights from multiple vantage points; and 3) a mechanism that encodes specific local 3D features within a broader multi-view framework. Experimental results confirm that our method quantitatively and qualitatively surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques on benchmark data. To validate spatial consistency, we extended the approach to dynamic scenarios. Finally, we demonstrated our method using a real-world multi-camera setup, proving it can achieve performance similar to multi-view photogrammetry while utilizing dramatically fewer images.

Standard image classification pipelines typically utilize a convolutional feature extractor linked with fully connected classification units, representing both predicted outputs and ground truth labels as one-hot vectors. This standard approach treats all categorical labels as having equal semantic distinction, overlooking the inherent visual relationships and hierarchical structures that define classes. We introduce an architecture featuring a Latent Hierarchy (LH) classifier that supersedes these traditional fully connected layers, coupled with an end-to-end learned mapping from Class2Str to uncover latent taxonomic structures. Evaluating on leading CFFAR and ImageNet models, our proposed LH classifier achieves parity or surpasses their accuracy in the ImageNet setting while utilizing significantly fewer parameters. Unlike prior hierarchical approaches (e.g., HDCNN) that generally constrain hierarchies to two levels, our method determines an optimal hierarchy without depth restrictions. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that closely related visually distinct categories naturally cluster within this learned hierarchy, mirroring real-world biological classifications.

Handling missing data within time series is a fundamental operational task for their analysis, where current approaches struggle with either irregular sampling or significantly degrade when observations are sparse. Addressing these limitations, this work reconstructs time series as permutation-equivariant sets and introduces NRTSI, a pioneering imputation model devoid of any recurrent structures. By leveraging this formulation, we have developed the highly efficient and theoretically principled NRTSI procedure to address data imputation systematically. Furthermore, NRTSI can directly manage time series with unevenly spaced samples, execute multi-mode stochastic completion, and cope with scenarios where only partial dimension data is observed. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that on a comprehensive suite of imputation benchmarks for time series, the method yields performance that rivals the current state-of-the-art standards.

An extended mean-field analysis (e-MFA), including quark one-loop vacuum fluctuations, has been utilized to calculate the vacuum effective potential and map the phase diagrams within the three-flavor (2+1) quark-meson model using various renormalization prescriptions to fix parameters. It was discovered that employing the quark-meson model with the vacuum term (QMVT) under a minimal subtraction scheme—where scalar and pseudo-scalar meson curvature masses determine parameters—is inconsistent, since these masses are defined as self-energies evaluated at zero momentum. This study marks the initial implementation of the consistent on-shell parameter fixing approach for the three-flavor quark-meson model. Consequently, the renormalized quark-meson (RQM) model relations physical meson pole masses for $\pi, K, \eta, \eta'$, along with scalar $\sigma$ mesons, the pion decay constant, and the kaon decay constant, by linking them to coupling and running mass parameters via on-shell or minimal subtraction schemes. Notably, plots of the nonstrange direction normalized vacuum effective potential align precisely for both the RQM and QMVT models when the $\sigma$ meson mass ($m_\sigma$) equals 658.8 MeV. Similarly, the order parameter temperature variations and resultant phase diagrams coincide between RQM and the pseudo-quark-meson variant (PQMVT) when the $\sigma$ meson mass is lowered by 10 MeV ($648$ MeV), driven largely by the interdependence of variations in the nonstrange and strange effective potential directions upon normalization in the nonstrange direction.

Although Multiplicative Error Models (MEMs) are frequently applied to real-valued time series, their inherent multiplication mechanism prevents their use on discrete count data without compromising the integer integrity of the statistics. To address this, we introduce a novel multiplicative operator tailored for counts, alongside specific implementations of this operator that form the basis of new Multiplicative Error Models for counts, known as CMEMs. When CMEMs are paired with a linear conditional mean, they align closely with integer-valued generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (INGARCH) models and can function as a semi-parametric extension of them. We characterize key stochastic properties across different INGARCH-CMEM variants and detail estimation strategies using both quasi-maximum likelihood and weighted least squares methods. Finally, the efficacy and application potential of these models are validated through extensive simulations and analyses of two real-world datasets.

Ensuring safety and reliability in autonomous driving relies heavily on high-accuracy localization. Achieving this is particularly vital for collective perception, an approach that utilizes C2X networks to exchange information among Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAV)s to enhance overall road safety. In such scenarios, minimal deviations in localization between CAVs can severely impede effective information fusion. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel method leveraging RANSAC (RANdom SAmple Consensus) specifically designed to correct relative positioning discrepancies between two CAVs and streamline their information exchange. Unlike conventional LiDAR localization techniques that depend solely on static environmental features, this framework exploits dynamic objects by leveraging real-time data exchange to refine localization. Specifically, while retaining traditional static landmarks like poles, fences, and walls as key matching points, the system also incorporates the centers of detected moving vehicles from both point clouds. Results from evaluations on the synthetic dataset COMAP indicate that, provided sufficient vehicle traffic and accurate detection of static poles by both units, the technique can reduce positional offsets to under 20 cm. Furthermore, the method demonstrates significant runtime efficiency, making it well-suited for practical real-time applications.

Segmentation, a foundational domain across both computer vision and natural language processing, serves to label individual pixels or features in order to identify regions of interest. The standard metrics for evaluating these tasks remain the Dice coefficient and Intersection over Union (IoU), which quantify the alignment between predictions and ground truth labels. Drawing on concepts analogous to calibration or Fisher consistency in classification, we develop a theoretical basis for Dice and IoU-guided segmentation. By leveraging Bayes rules, we rigorously prove that nearly all current operating losses based on simple thresholding frameworks are inconsistent with these metrics, potentially resulting in suboptimal outcomes. To resolve this issue, we introduce a novel consistent framework, termed RankDice or RankIoU. Drawing inspiration from plug-in estimators for Bayes segmentation, we design this ranking-based approach specifically tailored to the requirements of image and text segmentation. Furthermore, we have created three numeric algorithms capable of parallel GPU execution within both large-scale and high-dimensional contexts, alongside an analysis of the proposed framework’s statistical attributes. The method is confirmed to be both Dice- and IoU-consistent, with established excess risk bounds defined further. Empirical demonstrations using simulated scenarios and state-oftheart deep learning models show the efficacy of RankDice across Fine-anneated CitySclapes and PascalVOC datasets.

Hyperparameter optimization involves determining the most suitable configuration settings for a machine learning model within a specific learning task. While exhaustive search methods work for smaller datasets, they become the primary computational bottleneck when facing increased data volume and model complexity. A promising solution to this challenge is surrogate-based optimization. This approach utilizes a progressively updated model representing the relationship between the hyperparameter space and the desired output; data for this model comes from evaluating the main learning system—such as a factorization machine-based model—allowing the system to approximate the hyperparameter-output link. This surrogate model can then score numerous hyperparameter configurations, exploring areas of the space that are beyond the direct evaluation capabilities of the main engine. Typically, a surrogate model is chosen before initialization and remains fixed during the search. This study examined whether dynamically switching surrogates during optimization offers practical benefits for identifying optimal factorization machine-based models in the context of large-scale online recommendations. Benchmarks involving hundreds of millions of instances were conducted against established baselines using surrogates like Random Forests and Gaussian Processes. The outcomes demonstrate that switching surrogates during the process can achieve strong performance while reducing the required number of learning engine evaluations.

The approach applies a first transformation to dismantle inherent patterns in the data, followed by recycling a second permutation via a circulant-shift mechanism to generate the necessary $K$ hash values, which can reach magnitudes such as $24$. Surprisingly, the authors established that the estimator's variance under C-MinHash is fundamentally more compact than the variance derived in the classic MinHash framework. Li et al. also proved the indispensable utility of the initial perturbation in C-MinHash for theoretical clarity. Building upon these foundations but achieving greater practical efficiency we assert that the initial processing and the hash generation can both utilize an identical permutation, thus simplifying C-MinHash from requiring just  to a singular transformation that serves double duty. While deriving explicit theoretical expressions for the estimator's expectation necessitates considerable mathematical complexity, we successfully delineate the formulation while proving it is biased. Effective Reinforcement Learning systems require the ability to determine which historical events influenced observed results, a challenge termed credit assignment. Often, eligibility traces solve this by assigning credit based on a weighted set of recent experiences. Yet in complex tasks, recently experienced events merely represent a fraction of all possible actions that may have preceded the present outcome. Consequently, Reinforcement Learning can be enhanced by extending credit assignment over any viable preceding state, not just the immediately prior history. Accordingly, we explore "Predecessor Features," a fully bootstrapped evolution of van Hasselt's "Expected Trace," which facilitates such expanded credit assignment. An approach rooted in representing the anticipated sum of past state visitations, Predecessor Features enable Temporal Difference (TD) error signals to distribute more accurately across a broader array of ancestor states, significantly accelerating learning speeds compared to traditional strategies. Moreover, the algorithm inherently scales from discrete tabular representations to feature-based systems, boosting effectiveness across diverse environments. Detailed use cases and performance evaluations are provided comparing this method against existing alternatives.

Graph computation, essential for unlocking potential in domains ranging from social networking to web search within the big data landscape, faces challenges with frequent random memory calls and uneven workload distribution inherent in irregular network structures. Addressing this, we present an RCM-based preprocessing technique that enhances memory localization and ensures efficient workload balancing specifically for the BFS kernel. Additionally, we accelerate BFS computations running on the resulting RCM-ordered data using SIMD instructions. Experimental results derived from both Kronecker Graph files (Graph50 benchmark) and authentic real-world datasets confirm the approach's high performance, with our ARMv8-based implementation of BFS reaching remarkable energy efficiency levels and securing second place on the 2011 Green50 chart (with first position held by GPU-based acceleration).

The interaction between magnetic impurities and vortices in topological superconductors holds significant fundamental interest and critical implications for the development of quantum computing systems. Due to the coexistence of multiple degrees of freedom—specifically Majorana zero modes (MZMs), Caroli de Gennes Matricalon (CdGM) states, and bulk Cooper pair states—all interacting with impurities, isolating an impurity-in-vortex state has proven elusive. We provide an accurate theoretical solution to this challenge using a generalized mapping scheme combined with density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) methods. Our analysis identifies distinct in-gap states separate from the traditional Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) spectrum. These newly discovered in-gap phenomena are governed by three primary mechanisms: (i) the interplay between the impurity and bulk states, creating a competition between Cooper pairing and Kondo screening that yields a singlet-to-doublet quantum phase transition, (ii) the interaction between the impurity and CdGM states, which generates an effective Zeeman split for the doublet, and (iii) the entanglement between the impurity and MZMs, transforming that quantum phase transition into a smooth crossover. Collectively, these effects produce a unique spin-resolved local density of states. Notably, even in the vicinity of an MZM, our study predicts the emergence of a robust peak near zero energy, featuring height comparable to the MZM peak but with opposite spin polarization. These findings reveal new emergent physical properties that aid in interpreting complex experimental observations.

Magnetic skyrmions hold significant promise for energy-efficient computing because of their mobility, detectability, and non-volatility. Although a recent proposal based on reversible computing allows for circuits composed of directly cascaded skyrmion logic gates, this method is hampered by the high energy costs and manufacturing challenges linked to using notches for synchronization. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel skyrmion logic approach synchronized through voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy (VCMA). We support this by demonstrating the principles of VCMA synchronization in micromagnetic simulations, while also evaluating the effects of anisotropy barrier height, current density, and skyrmion velocity on their movement. Furthermore, additional simulations confirm the viability of cascaded logic circuits where VCMA synchronized modules facilitate clocking and pipelining, establishing a feasible path toward large-scale, energy-efficient computing architectures built on magnetic skyrmions.

Discrete Fracture Networks (DFNs) are intricate three-dimensional constructs formed by the intersection of polygonal, planar fractures, serving to simulate fluid flow within fractured formations. Although Domain Decomposition (DD) techniques are well-suited to such systems, research数量有限 specifically on implementing these methods for DFNs remains scarce. This study conducts a theoretical analysis regarding the application of Optimized Schwarz Methods (OSMs) to DFNs and demonstrates, under specific domain decomposition conditions and associated assumptions, their weak scalable capabilities—meaning iteration counts converge to required tolerances regardless of the number of fractures included. This finding resonates with the growing attention given to the weak scalability of DD algorithms in specific geometries and environments where coarse spaces may be unnecessary. While the analysis involves assumptions about practical applicability limitations that require further validation, it nonetheless offers actionable guidance for mitigating computational costs. Furthermore, we underscore that this framework can be effortlessly adapted to examine additional conventional DD approaches when addressing DFN problems.

We introduce a novel 'Import Resonance' (IR) mechanism, wherein coupling strength creates an information-import maximum, complementary to the existing Recurrence Resonance (RR)—a peak in state correlation and mutual information driven by specific noise amplitudes. Ultimately SGDraw allows for improving accuracy and efficiency of complex tasks in machine vision.

Although strong magnetic fields are prevalent in many degenerate stellar remnants, their evolutionary origins and developmental paths remain largely unclear. New findings from volume-limited surveys indicate a diverse phenomenon rather than one uniform process. Among high-mass white dwarfs, likely formed from mergers, we observe extremely strong and frequent magnetic fields that manifest at the very onset of cooling, suggesting generation by merging-driven dynamo activity. In contrast, low-mass white dwarfs born from single star evolution typically emerge non-magnetic and weakly develop detectable fields at low intensities, observed in only about a quarter of cases; these may originate internally during early development and gradually rise to the surface. Additionally, field strength and prevalence increase as the stars cool, eventually reaching the levels seen in the most massive stars after they surpass the point of core crystallization. This effect hints at an internal dynamo operation analogous to Earth's.

When deploying neural networks (NNs) in critical applications such as healthcare, accurately quantifying uncertainty in black-box architectures is indispensable. Although recent studies utilizing Bayesian and non-Bayesian techniques have established methods for unified predictive uncertainty modeling, breaking this uncertainty down to isolate specific sources of data heteroscedasticity offers richer insights into root causes. To this end, we introduce the **deep split ensemble**, a straightforward non-Bayesian method that disentangles predictive uncertainty via a multivariate Gaussian mixture model. In our approach, neural networks are conditioned on input features that have first been grouped into clusters, generating uncertainty estimates specific to each cluster. Our proposed methodology was evaluated across multiple benchmark regression datasets, further contrasting performance against unified uncertainty baselines. Extensive analyses utilizing the empirical Rule of Three and dataset splits confirm that the models are inherently well-calibrated. Additionally, we validated our approach in a multimodal context using the benchmark Alzheimer''s disease dataset, demonstrating its ability to reveal latent biases specific to certain modality types. Given the minimal adjustments required for both architecture and training methodology, combined with the high flexibility offered by clustering schemes, the method is both highly deployable and versatile. Source code can be found at https://github.com/wazeerzulfikar/deep-split-ensembles.

Experimental simulations reveal modest gains for disease reduction via contact tracing only under low observation conditions. In contrast, halting disease dissemination necessitates both high visibility thresholds of the contact network and the capacity to restrict approximately fifty percent of the population. Crucially, proactively isolating "super-links"—critical proximity encounters, offers significant advantages. Specifically targeting one quarter of the population achieves a 35% visibility rate, which can forestall the escalation of an epidemic. Evidence suggests that while isolating super-spreaders is more effective traditional contact tracing and diagnostics, they yield inferior results compared to specifically isolating super-links. Moreover, network architecture plays an existential role in the course of an epidemic. We propose a proactive intervention framework involving the strategic deactivation of both super-spreader nodes and critical transmission edges. In conclusion, removing these high-connectivity hubs to proactively immunize segments of the population should serve as an effective adjunct alongside conventional contact tracing and testing within a robust and sophisticated public health strategy for epidemic responses, showcasing the significance of network topology.

Mixed Reality (MR) technologies can transform the Internet of a future generation through highly immersive metaverse services, yet achieving satisfactory user satisfaction depends critically on synchronizing digital models with their physical counterparts. To this end, this study introduces an integrated framework for sampling, communication, and prediction, aiming to reduce communication burdens while strictly limiting the Mean Squared Error (MSE)—a measure of tracking fidelity—between physical devices and their digital avatars. Leveraging domain-specific expert data to determine ideal sampling rates and forecasting horizons, we engineered the Knowledge-assisted Constrained Twin-Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (KC-TD3) algorithm. Testing on a physical-kinetic prototype featuring a robotic arm and its virtual replica yielded several key results: (1) Under tight tracking error constraints (MSE at 0.002 degrees), the framework naturally simplifies to a sampling-communication co-design model. (2), Under relaxed constraints (MSE at 0.007 degrees), it simplifies to a prediction-communication co-design model. (3) The system offers a superior balance between tracking accuracy and data traffic, reducing average communication load by an observed factor; specifically, by 87%, to satisfy stricter error margins of 0.002 degrees—a significant improvement over systems lacking sampling and predictive elements. (4), The proposed approach surpasses traditional methods using fixed, statically optimized parameters derived from exhaustive search, specifically regarding the tail probabilities of tracking error. Additionally, by incorporating expert guidance into the KC-TD3 algorithm, we observed enhanced convergence speed, greater operational stability, and overall improved performance.

The swift expansion of the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoTiT) has positioned embedded systems as critical targets for both security professionals and malicious actors. These embedded devices, characterized by non-standard hardware and heterogeneous software, create distinct obstacles for researchers analyzing firmware binaries. The tight coupling between firmware and diverse hardware components significantly hinders dynamic analysis in virtualized settings; however, attempting to emulate a vast range of hardware peripherals often necessitates frequently rewriting emulators for different firmware environments, severely constraining analytical efficiency. 

This study focuses on a firmware re-hosting approach involving real-time operating systems (RTOSs). Typically, developers construct a BSP and associated device drivers for their platforms. We propose that by supplying high-fidelity substitutions for these specific routines and drivers, we can migrate minimal changes to firmware when moving from native hardware to virtualization. We demonstrate a methodology that scales firmware execution by automatically patching binaries, eliminating the need to modify existing emulators. Titled static binary-level porting, this technique identifies BSP and driver components within the target firmware and patches them to align with pre-built drivers and BSP routines adapted for current emulators. We validate the utility of this method across multiple hardware platforms and diverse firmware samples for security evaluation, showing its flexibility in facilitating vulnerable system assessment and exploit generation.

Verifying multiplier designs correctly and with efficiency, particularly using rigorously sound methodologies, presents a significant challenge. This work demonstrates how the ACL2 theorem prover was utilized to construct an optimized rewriting algorithm specifically for verifying multiplier designs. By leveraging a fundamental comprehension of ACL2's features and internal data structures, we developed a validated program capable of automatically confirming diverse multiplier designs at speeds exceeding those of current leading tools. Furthermore, our system grants users the flexibility to modify specifications, enabling verification of different multiplier variants. We also elaborate on the challenges overcome during development, offering insights into implementation details crucial for both system verifiability and operational efficiency. This discourse provides valuable advantages both for those aiming to deploy efficient programs within theorem proving frameworks and those interested in adapting our multiplier verification approach to other architectures.

Electroencephalography (EEG) is a favored and efficient tool for detecting emotions; however, the mechanisms by which EEG signals propagate within the human brain, as well as their inherent correlation with emotions, remain poorly understood among researchers. To better investigate the relationship between these spatial and temporal EEG features and emotion, this work introduces four distinct transformer architectures: spatial attention, temporal attention, sequential spatial-temporal attention, and simultaneous spatial-temporal attention. Individual use of spatial attention captures topological information suited to emotion recognition, while temporal attention isolates time-varying EEG traits specifically for emotional analysis. Sequential spatial-temporal attention applies spatial attention over one-electrode segment within a specific time frame followed by temporal attention across samples, aiming to gauge how strong an emotional stimulus impacts EEG signals at diverse electrodes within a given time period. In contrast, the proposed methodology utilizes simultaneous spatial-temporal attention to execute these tasks at the same time, modeling how spatial features correlate during various temporal segments. Experimental findings reveal that the proposed approach using simultaneous spatial and temporal attention yields superior emotion recognition accuracy, demonstrating that capturing the correlations among EEG signals' temporal and spatial features is crucial.

Active search within adaptive experimental design involves locating scarce, high-value items within the limits of a finite budget. A critical factor in this domain is the diversity of selected targets, as varying discoveries typically yield deeper insights for subsequent applications. Currently, prevailing search algorithms generally classify all targets as positive or rely on basic heuristics for diversity promotion without adequate versatility. We introduce an innovative framework for active search across multiple distinct classes of targets, leveraging a utility function selected from an expansive family that fosters diversity by capitalizing on diminishing returns. Under a Bayesian analytical framework, we establish a hardness theorem that precludes the approximation of optimal strategies using arbitrary utilities that are positive, monotonic increasing, concave. Furthermore, we develop a precise yet computationally efficient, nonmyopic algorithm approximated for these specific utility classes. It is empirically shown in diverse environments, including drug development scenarios, to outperform current methods empirically.

Legal officials prioritized cannabis legalization driven by strong advocacy suggesting mental health improvements, yet early scientific evidence remains inconclusive. This study examines the relationship between depression and cannabis use within a targeted social media corpus focusing on users consuming cannabis to enhance their mental health. Tweets from the dataset include three independently verified annotations by experts: Reason, Effect, and Addiction. Conventional natural language processing methods fail to adequately extract the connections between depression markers and cannabis references. Consequently, we propose a methodology incorporating specialized knowledge, integrating the Drug Abuse Ontology for addiction with Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders lexicons. Given constraints on expert annotations, we implemented a supervised contrastive learning approach alongside GPT-3, pre-trained on an extensive corpus to maximize performance even with restricted labeled data. Experimental findings demonstrate our method significantly outperforms standard relation extractors in isolating cannabis-depression links. Furthermore, a learned nearest-neighbor mechanism can generate reliable high-quality annotations, equipping the research community to better understand the complexities of this association when expert labeling resources remain scarce.

Recent breakthroughs in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) highlight the effectiveness of transferable prototypical learning in facilitating conditional alignment, specifically by drawing cross-domain class centroids closer. Nevertheless, inner-class compactness and subtle, fine-grained subtype structures within these domains remain insufficiently addressed and explore here. We introduce an adapted strategy for fine-grained subtype-aware alignment, leveraging intermediate pseudo labels to simultaneously maximize separation between classes while ensuring tightness amongst distinct subtypes. The rationale leverages findings that while unlabeled subtypes of the same class may diverge due to varying data and label discrepancies to one another, they maintain intrinsic proximity to each. We examine the effectiveness of this method in handling cases both where and where subtype counts are unknown, enabling the discovery of subtype structures concurrently. The developed subtype-conscious dynamic UDA framework delivers encouraging outcomes for medical diagnosis applications.

In various practical contexts, machine learning training data arrive progressively; however, neural networks frequently encounter a challenge known as *catastrophic forgetting*, wherein they assimilate new concepts but retain less of previously acquired information. Preventing this issue is notoriously arduous under practical constraints such as storage bandwidth and computational limitations. Furthermore, initializing large-scale models, notably Transformers, from scratch is expensive and demands extensive labeled data that may be scarce in specific application areas. Although emerging research suggests reducing this problem effectively via expanding-parameter dynamic architectures, current methods are complex to calibrate to balance parameter growth with cross-task sharing, leading to substantial overheads and scalability challenges for tasks. Consequently, this study empirically validated the Adaptive Distillation of Adapters (ADA)—originally designed for text classification employing pre-trained Transformer-adaptations within continual learning—in a computer vision context. Findings confirm that ADA sustains superior predictive accuracy over sequential classification benchmarks and expands execution histories without necessitating model retraining or increasing parameter count. Additionally, this method surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions regarding inference efficiency.

Through the incorporation of electron screening methods based on our extended version of the Koopmans' equation, we successfully describe band-gap opening across both weakly- and strongly-acting correlation regimes in materials such as bulk LiH, Si; as well as both paramagnetic NiO and antiferromagnetic NiO. Notwithstanding some inaccuracies remaining within the complete photoemission spectra, this finding is significant as a fully self-consistent electronic structure simulation result that provides the groundwork towards unified modeling for photoemission spectra in extremes of weak to strong correlation.

Game theoretical approaches have garnered significant attention for handling planning and prediction within complex multi-agent settings; however, they often presuppose a solitary local Nash equilibrium, thereby failing to account for uncertainties regarding agent intentions. Although maximum entropy (MaxEnt) dynamic games aim to resolve these limitations, existing practical methodologies typically resolve MaxEnt equilibria through linear-quadratic approximations. This restricts them to modeling only unimodal reactions and renders them ill-suited for contexts characterized by multiple local Nash equilibria. Through a reformulation of the problem as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), we introduce MPOGames, an efficient solution method for optimizing interactions across multiple local Nash equilibria in MaxEnt dynamic games. We further demonstrate the critical value of game theoretic techniques informed by uncertainty analysis using a case study involving a merging scenario between two agents. Lastly, hardware experiments conducted on a 1/10th scale automobile platform substantiate our approach's real-time performance.

Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are a prominent approach for extracting low-dimensional structures from high-dimensional data, becoming essential for data exploration and scientific breakthrough. Yet, scientific workflows differ from standard machine learning tasks; unlike training a single model on one dataset repeatedly, this context prioritizes learned features that are adaptable across labs, reproducible, and suitable for integrating incremental data. Ideally, disparate research teams should yield comparable results without explicitly exchanging fully trained models or complete data repositories. This study tackles that goal via the Rosetta VAE (R-VAE), a technique to distill prior representation-learning and retrain new models to reconstruct previous work. R-VAE employs clustering within the latent space of a pre-trained network to detect specific latent input pairs known as Rosetta Points, establishing anchors for future training. By using an adjustable hyperparameter, $\rho$, the method trades off between preserving the original latent space geometry and incorporating new data. Empirical results confirm that R-VAE matches the data reconstruction quality and performance of standard VAs and $\beta$-VAEs but significantly improves recovery consistency within the latent space across sequel training iterations and ensures greater consistency of the learned representations over different runs.

This work investigates the mean-field dynamics of broad many-body systems featuring stochastic fluctuations in their interactions. Our analysis demonstrates a universal power-law decay of the order parameter, given by $m(t)\sim t^{-\chi}$ with $\chi=\frac{1}{3}$. This exponent remains invariant regardless of most system-specific details, such as stochastic driving strength, the energy spectra undriven systems would possess without driving, initial configurations, or the specific protocols employed. We show that this dynamical universality arises from a diffusion process characterized by a time-dependent diffusion coefficient, evolving self-consistently. Finally, the implications regarding finite-size effects and empirical validation in contemporary high-finesse cavity QED experiments are examined.

Lusztig's faux degree serves as a generating polynomial enumerating the major indices for standard Young tableaux of any specific shape. Building on findings by James & Kerber and Springer, it is striking—though not immediately obvious—that evaluating this polynomial at a $k$-th primitive root of unity returns the count of border strip tableaux containing only strips of size $k$, possibly adjusted by a sign. This phenomenon corresponds largely to the Murnaghan-Nakayama rule, which calculates the value of an irreducible symmetric group character at a rectangular partition by focusing solely on these specific tableaux. We now refine this theorem to accommodate a specific descent count within standard and border strip tableaux. To achieve this, wedefine a fresh statistic of descent tailored to border strip tableaux, which generalizes the traditional concept of descent applied to standard forms. Although Deep Reinforcing Reinforcement Learning has recently advanced across different domains, effectively interpreting the behavior of RL agents remains a challenging open problem largely due to the intricacy of deciphering neural network decisions. While prior research has turned toward decision-tree-based models to foster policy explainability—specifically utilizing Soft Decision Trees (SDTs) and differentiable discretized Decision Trees (DDTs), both of which demonstrate a balance of strong performance and explainability—this paper proposes Cascading Decision Trees (CDTs) for further advancement. By applying learned representation techniques to the paths within decision trees and allowing a richer structure to emerge during approximation and explanation phases. Extensive assessments of these tools, where they served as both surrogate surrogate policy models and imitation learners attempting to explain behavior from non-interpretable policies, showed they significantly strengthened the performance of existing methods, achieving more precise, high-quality models that captured the essential information underlying the behavior patterns exhibited and could be easily followed. A key finding also highlighted that even with tree-based models capable of producing such transparent results as policies, using them via the process of imitation still faced limitations due to inherent instability in accurately reflecting the true decision-making logic when bridged between non-explainable and explainable architectures.

Traditional super-resolution (SR) techniques frequently rely on the assumption that low-resolution (LR) counterparts are formed downscaling an unknown high-resolution (HR) source using a static, ideal kernel such as bicubic filtering. In practice, however, LR capture conditions vary wildly from synthetic datasets used in research. When this assumption clashes reality, standard SR performance drops precipitously, giving birth to "Blind SR," where the downscaling mechanism ("SR kernel") remains unseen. Previous work demonstrated that the optimal SR-ner is the one maximizing cross-scale recurrence of image patches within the LR content. In this study, we demonstrate how leveraging deep internal learning can harness this cross-scale recurrence. Specifically, we present KernelGAN, an image-conditional internal Generative Adversarial Network. It undergoes training exclusively on the input LR test image during inference, effectively modeling its internal texture and distribution statistics. In this architecture, a Generator learns to create artificially downscaled versions that remain statistically indistinguishable from the true downscaled patches according to a matching Discriminator. Following convergence, this Generator serves as the engine implementing the downscaling process controlled by a precise, image-specific SR-kernel. As a completely self-training, unsupervised approach requiring no external supervision datasets beyond the input itself, KernelGANG integrates with existing SR frameworks to yield leading results in Blind-SR applications.

As growth temperatures drop, this 30° domain grows in proportion to the direct (0°) alignment; we attribute this shift to reduced surface mobility at lower heat, which promotes remote growth, whereas high heat facilitates faster surface diffusion that supports pinhole-driven epitaxis. The observation of this 30° superstructure serves as an experimental signature for remote epitaxis, uniquely ruling out the primary alternative mechanisms discussed earlier.

Certifying the resilience of deep learning models critically depends on adversarial perturbations. Since universal adversarial perturbations (UAPs) can target multiple images simultaneously with a unified threat model, they eliminate the need for image-specific attack procedures. However, current UAP generator tools often underperform when processing images from diverse sources with varying resolutions. To achieve genuine versatility across image sources, we conceptualize UAP generation through the lens of few-shot learning, utilizing learning-to-optimize (L2O) and bilevel optimization strategies to enhance attack success rates (ASR). Initially, the prevalent model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) framework is applied to train a universal perturbation generator in meta-learning scenarios. However, MAML alone cannot directly facilitate universal attacks across diverse sources. Therefore, the study integrates MAML within the L2O framework to create a superior approach that:
1) outperforms baseline methods such as Projected Gradient Descent by achieving a 50% increase in attack success;
2) delivers efficiency gains, operating 37% faster than standard vanilla L2O or standalone MAML frameworks where possible; and
3) effectively generates UAPs adaptable to various target models and differing image data sources.

This study aims to optimize receiver placement for the most effective tracking of tagged marine wildlife. The core objective is to identify deployment positions that maximize coverage, balancing the risk of inaccurate tracking caused by overly dense stations against the limited coverage resulting from sparse ones. We formulate receiver siting as a constrained, non-convex optimization problem that accounts for tag specifications and local geography, proposing a computationally efficient sub-optimal solution scalable to large networks. Simulation tests across three virtual aquatic environments show the method expands localization coverage by 30%, while real-world experiments validate similar performance. Furthermore, we open-source our implementation to facilitate the establishment of custom acoustic observatories by researchers worldwide.

Gaussian Graphical Models (GGM) are frequently employed in neuroimaging research involving fMRI, EEG, or MEG data to gauge functional connectivity and relationships among distant brain areas. When analyzing groups separately in multi-subject studies, researchers aim to detect significant differences in the functional links between patients and healthy controls, necessitating large-scale inference across network edges after graph model selection—a task we termed the Population Post Selection Inference problem. Existing methodologies typically predict an individual graph for each participant, treat these as fixed, and perform two-sample edge-level testing; however, ignoring the variance from estimating subject-specific graphs often leads to high false-positive rates and diminished statistical power. To address these limitations, our newly introduced procedure, named R³, utilizes a large-scale resampling technique with a group random-effects test statistic that properly accounts and averages the post-selection across subjects and individuals, allowing us to estimate inference variability after graph construction and eliminate these issues. Through simulations and by identifying whether functional links were added to autistic individuals' diagrams, our method demonstrated significant improvement in power and error control to support the analysis of multi-subjects based fMRI data ABIDE studies.

Numerical modeling for fluid and solute transport in porous media frequently relies on hybrid-dimensional frameworks, where fractures are represented as lower-dimensional entities relative to the matrix. These models typically utilize non-conforming discretizations to circumvent complex mesh generation issues at fracture-matrix interfaces; however, they necessitate intricate sub-model coupling and specific measures to guarantee flux conservation. We introduce a novel methodology based on modeling fractures with equal dimensional representation to the matrix. Overcoming the principal challenge of resolving complex fracture-matrix interfaces in equal dimensional formats requires an adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) approach. Our specific strategy starts with a coarse, uniform grid, then iteratively refines cells that have non-overlapping regions with fractures, resulting in non-uniform, non-conforming approximations capable of achieving high interface fidelity despite not resolving them explicitly. We demonstrate that low-order finite element schemes using these adaptive grids maintain both global and local conservation, and we modify an algebraic flux correction method to satisfy the discrete maximum principle, specifically adjusting rigorous M-matrix conditions for non-conforming basis functions. While the specific examples targeted geophysics, the methodology and findings are broadly applicable to various diffusion and transport problems across both conforming and non-conforming grid structures.

Functionalized nanoparticles (NPs), found across diverse systems ranging from synthetic particles to viruses, possess complex morphological structures with varying decorations. Consequently, standard modeling often treats these entities as simplified spheres in a first-approximation approach. At the nanoscale, modifications to particle morphology are expected to generate intricate hydrodynamic interactions, which become magnified when NPs are restricted or positioned near surfaces. While diffusion coefficients can estimate these mobility changes, accurately reproducing the hidden features caused non-simplified morphological aspects necessifies more advanced structural modeling. This study characterizes the passive transport of functionalized NP—both free within a volume and under confinement—using the Rigid Multi-Blob (RMB) method, which offers robust accuracy and efficiency in modeling complex nanoscale mobilities. Specifically, research was conducted to determine how the distribution, size, and shapes of functional clusters impact nanoparticle rotational and translational diffusion. Findings reveal that functional clusters significantly impede rotational diffusion; a NP with multiple and specifically configured morphological groups exhibits notable mobility reductions relative to non-functional counterparts. Furthermore, confinement introduces marked modifications to diffusivity and leaves unique marks on off-diagonal components of rotational diffusion. Leveraging these insights can enhance applications across imaging fields, drug transport, medical treatment design, and the engineering of polymer-based composites.

The robust quantitative and qualitative findings demonstrate that our approach yields consistent performance gains relative to baseline counterparts. Furthermore, this method successfully won the FetReg Endovis Sub-challenge on Semantic Segmentation, organized as a part of MICCAI 2021.

We introduce a new and resilient framework capable of generating both data-free and universally applicable coresets under minimal weight assumptions while requiring no data constraints at all. Our core method determines neuron importance based on the subsequent layer's outputs and relies on the integration of Löwner-John ellipsoids and Carathéodory's theorem as of our technique. Being data-free and easily adapted to different datasets, we present a robust method for DNN compression. Our experimental findings underscore our method's superiority in pruning performance compared with current approaches. Our method further demonstrates its effectiveness by enabling up to a 62 percent compression rate on ResNet50 within the ImageNet dataset while maintaining a modest accuracy loss of approximately 1.09%.

Discovering an intermediate-mass black hole (IBH) population in the $10^2-10^6\ M_\odot$ range could reveal their formation contexts—such as active galactic nuclei disks or globular clusters—and shed light on how supermassive black holes form. While ground-based detectors have identified one candidate event involving an IBH progenitor of approximately $142^{+28}_{-16}\ M_\odot$, their search sensitivity is hampered by short-term, incoherent noise in local data that can imitate these gravitational-wave signals. In this work, we applied a Bayesian-inspired statistic, designed to assess the coherency of triggers across multiple sensors, to search for binary black hole mergers in LIGO's second observing run, targeting systems with lab-frame masses exceeding $\gtrsim 55\ M_\odot$. Our findings did not confirm any additional intermediate-mass black holes; instead, we identified several stellar-massa binary black hole candidates that were absent from the first Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog (GWTC-1).

Data augmentation methods have become central to improving the decoding of electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. In response to these shortcomings, this paper presents a novel target-centered subject transfer framework designed for data augmentation. The process involves constructing a curated subset of source data with maximized relevance to the target domain, followed by the application of a generative model to facilitate this data transfer to the target. Unlike conventional methods, this proposed framework enhances target domain explainability through supplementary real data augmentation rather than noise, yielding superior performance when contrasted with other augmentation strategies. Furthermore, extensive experimentation confirms the approach's high robustness and efficacy, establishing it as a potent tool for advancing future research in this domain.

This method identifies a limited number of highly representative and instructive triplets through an iterative process involving two primary stages: first, utilizing an iterative algorithm to pick anchor images that exhibit maximum diversity within an embedded space; second, assigning varied sets of positive and negative counterparts to each anchor based on a new strategic assessment of their relevancy, hardness, and mutual diversity. The source code developed by the researchers is open and accessible on GitHub at https://git.tu-berlin.de/rsim/image-retrieval-from-triplets (https).

Condensing atmospheric moisture on surfaces represents a promising method to tackle the global potable water shortage. However, significant research questions remain regarding the underlying physical processes of this condensation, specifically how it diverges from pure steam dynamics in humid air. Clarifying these mechanisms and identifying ideal surface wettability and operational modes are crucial for optimizing water harvesting performance. This study attributes the prevailing ambiguity primarily to distinct heat transfer characteristics between condensing from pure vapor versus humid air. Notably, when condensing from humid air, thermal resistance within the water layer does not dominate; instead, the process is regulated by vapor diffusion and the drainage of liquid. These findings indicate that filmwise condensation paired with superhydrophilic surfaces maximizes water retrieval rates. Experimental validation involved measuring condensation rates across various superhydrophilic and superhydrophobic substrates over a temperature range of 5 to 56 K difference and humidity variations ranging from 5 to 45 grams of water per kilogram of dry air. Results demonstrated that superhydrophilic surfaces yielded 57% to 333% higher condensation rates compared to superhydrophobic counterparts. Ultimately, this research challenges a century of uncertainty surrounding the physics of vapor condensation in moist environments, paving the way for the development of more effective atmospheric water harvesting technologies.

Performing multi-step intensive manipulation procedures, like prying and twisting open a push-and-turn child resistant bottle, mandates robots navigate complex planning decisions deeply rooted in the necessity to apply physical force. These decisions span discrete and continuous variables involving both the sequencing of operations—such as the binary choice of whether to pick up an item—and the continuous parameters of those actions. To facilitate planning and the precise execution of force-driven tasks, an advanced task and motion planner is extended with specific kinematic chain constraints designed to explicitly model frictional bounds and applied torque via a new "forceful" approach. Across three application scenarios—involving bottle opening, nuts being twisted down, and vegetable cutting—the study shows how the method selects optimal strategies from a vast set of combinatorial options. Additionally, cost-weighted optimization is demonstrated to identify robust parameter and procedural strategies even when faced with uncertainty in the physical properties of the environment.

To combat the COVID-19 pandemic and suppress its outbreak, implementing physical social distancing as a mandatory non-pharmaceutical measure helps decelerate SARS-COV-2 transmission among the population. Leverading support from the National Science Foundation (NSF), this initiative builds an interactive, web-native GIS platform that furnishes real-time quantitative data on citizen adherence to social distancing mandates across U.S. states and counties. By synthesizing daily human mobility patterns originating from massive datasets of anonymized, aggregate smart-phone GPS coordinates at the county level, the system strives to amplify community and governmental risks through increased awareness, informing public policy, and facilitating more robust community responses.

This study presents Koha, an overarching theory designed to resolve two lingering mysteries regarding biological neural circuits: the mechanisms by which information is housed and processed within these circuits, as well as how neurons evolve into pattern-detecting units. Within Koha, neural dendritic spines function as computational nodes that analyze their synaptic inputs for exact spike patterns. The theory posits an inherent temporal code in each dendritic spine, allowing it to modulate signal intensity through dampening or boosting based on specific timing cues from incoming spike trains. The work substantiates these claims by outlining how signals are filtered via spine necks and offers evidence of this mechanism in action. Drawing upon this framework, a proposed competitive learning algorithm describes how neurons harness their intrinsic temporal codes to develop into sophisticated pattern detectors.

The KM3NeT Collaboration is building an active, multi-site atmospheric neutrino observatory in the Mediterranean Sea, which utilizes arrays of pressure-resistant glass spheres, each equipped with thirty-one small-aperture photomultipliers. The primary scientific targets include identifying cosmic neutrino sources and determining atmospheric neutrino oscillation parameters. Detection methods involve capturing photons emitted via Cherenkov radiation, which are triggered by charged leptons generated from neutrino interactions in the surrounding water. To achieve the precise angular resolution essential to these goals, photomultiifiers across the array must maintain a time synchronization accuracy on the scale of approximately one nanosecond. To address the massive cost implications of such a vast volume, cost-efficiency has become a critical objective. Consequently, the KM3NeT Collaboration designed and created the low-cost Nanobeacons specifically for detector time calibration, with production exceeding 600 units. Since the optical pulse shape and wavelength emission characteristics determine the calibration effectiveness, these attributes are vital. The present paper details the key features of the Nanobeacons' design and deployment and examines the properties of the generated light pulses.

Support Vector Machine (SVM) modeling represents an effective classification strategy in machine learning that excels with small-sample forecasting issues in complex, high-dimensional settings; this technique was subsequently adapted for regression into Support Vector Regression (SVR), where the primary hurdle involves selecting suitable parameters. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel Support Vector Regression model optimized by a newly formulated Golden Sine Algorithm (GSA). We evaluate the proposed GSA-SVR system's efficacy against ten other competitive metaheuristic approaches using historical financial data of technological firms sourced from Yahoo Finance. Performance is assessed using Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Mean Absolute Percent Error (MAPE), revealing that the algorithm not only rivals existing methods but also demonstrates superior precision while maintaining efficient computational time.

The creation of virtual agents has made human-avatar interactions significantly more complex and engaging. Furthermore, virtual agents capable of naturally mimicking emotions strengthen the social bond between humans and intelligent machines, making their repertoire of non-verbal cues a vital element in human-machine communication. Laughter extends beyond a mere audio waveform, representing a multimodal form of communication that integrates both auditory elements along with specific facial gestures and body dynamics. Although motion analysis typically requires relevant motion capture databases, acquiring these datasets presents the significant hurdles of cost and time inefficiency. This research investigates how laughter relates to body movements within dyadic dialogues, extracting physical motions via deep-learning-based pose estimation. Results derived from the NDC-ME dataset indicate that one single joint movement statistic—such as the peak value derived either from raw data or its Fast Fourier Transform—correlates only slightly with laughter intensity, reaching roughly a 30% match. Conversely, no direct correlation exists between auditory features and physical movements, prompting a discussion on the difficulties in utilizing such datasets for tasks like audio-driven co-laughter motion synthesis.

This article investigates the sharpness of phase transitions within percolation models constructed upon planar spin systems. After examining in detail the Glauber dynamics of the Ising model as well as a Dynamic Bootstrap process, we demonstrate that the phase transitions for both are continuous and sharp, while also deriving quantitative estimates for two-point connectivity. Additionally, the techniques developed herein prove broadly useful for addressing various dependent percolation models, allowing us to identify related challenges. Finally, the concluding section outlines a comprehensive array of open problems that will demand novel approaches in the coming work.

This study examines the influence of quantum coherence on both closed and open quantum batteries, deriving upper limits on work performed or energy exchange based on coherence metrics. We demonstrate that energy storage capacity is bounded by the Hilbert-Schmidt coherence found in the density matrix when expressed within the spectral basis of the unitary operator governing the battery's evolution. Furthermore, we establish that a corresponding bound exists regarding battery Hamiltonian coherence relative to the same operator basis, determined via the commutator. These theoretical results are validated using a four-state quantum systems model, as well as applications involving the closed-system 4-state scenario with the anisotropic XY Ising model and the Spin-Boson model for the open quantum framework.

Optimization issues governed by PDEs are frequently handled via the reduced-formulation method, which eliminates PDE constraints and proves computationally more viable for large scales compared to alternatives. **Context:** Decades of robotic missions have significantly advanced our geological and geophysical knowledge of solar system small bodies, though these efforts have only targeted a fraction of such objects. The NASA Dawn mission stands among them for providing the first comprehensive maps of Vesta's (asteroid 4) topography and albedo at a ~20 m/pixel resolution.  

**Aims:** This study aims to assess what precision can be achieved when retrieving Vesta's surface topography and albedo using the VLT/SPHERE (ESO program), utilizing data from Dawns earlier space mission to serve as an independent benchmark.  

**Methods:** Over a six-visit period as part of the VLT/SPHERES ZIMPOL ESO observing run (Proposal ID: 199.c-077), we collected data on a series of six epochs and deproject the images with parametric PSF. Subsidarily, the spatial patterns we recorded were then juxtaposed against a simulated model derived from Dawns official Digital Elevation data set, to which we added an albedo overlay.  

**Results.** Analysis indicates that utilizing ground-based deconvolutions of VLT/SPHERES images produces a comparable imaging fidelity to space-based observations, retrieving primary surface morphology and albedo features with a ~20 --30km precision level. Plasma diagnostics form the foundation for studying the physical and chemical characteristics of gaseous systems that emit radiation through specific spectral lines. However, proper execution of such diagnostics requires the accurate correction of input spectra for attenuation (extinction), a necessity driven by the dependency on the gas's own physical properties. Consequently, extinction correction and plasma diagnostics must be conducted simultaneously in a self-consistent manner. By analyzing nine luminous planetary nebulae in M 31 with varying levels of attenuation correction and plasma diagnostics, the authors illustrate how using initial assumptions—particularly those inconsistent between these processes—can distort analytical outcomes. Specifically, they identify that the mass distribution in the M 31 sample, representing the high end of low-mass progenitor systems, follows expected theoretical predictions. Furthermore, the authors conclude that previous findings suggesting anomalous overabundant nitrogen in these Planetary Nebulae were primarily due to underestimated extinction caused by these inconsistent methods; this error propagated as systematic offsets in attenuation-corrected line strengths, thereby negatively impacting derived elemental and ionic ratios and leading to other flawed inferences. Broadly speaking, existing literature on plasma diagnostics that disregarded self-simultaneous alignment with attenuation corrections should be treated with caution, ideally undergoing re-evaluation to achieve full mutual consistency.

Reinforcement learning seeks to discover optimal policies by interacting with environments where the underlying dynamics are not known. Numerous approaches utilize the estimation of a value function to generate near-optimal policies. However, in partially observable settings these value functions are dependent on the full history of past actions and current observations. In this paper, the empirical investigation demonstrates that when recurrent neural networks learn these value functions to approximate Q-functions, the network's hidden representations effectively internalize the filtering of the posterior state distribution, formally known as belief. Specifically, our analysis reveals that, throughout the learning of the Q-function, the network's hidden layers become increasingly correlated with the specific belief variables that are critical for optimal control, a relationship quantified by increasing mutual information. Additionally, results indicate that an agent's anticipated return improves as its recurrent structure develops stronger mutual information between its hidden state and the agent's beliefs. Conversely, our experiments also show a reduction in mutual information concerning belief variables that are not essential for optimal control during the learning process. In essence, a recurrent neural network learning the Q-factor for a partially observable environment captures the core necessary beliefs from the full history without irrelevant information. By becoming correlated with the most critical state components for decision-making, its hidden memorizations essentially emulate a belief sufficient statistic for effective control.

In practical dialogue system applications, generated responses must meet multiple interrelated constraints: informativity, authenticity, and control. Both leading approaches to language generation—specifically rule-based systems and neural language modeling—are ineffective at fulfilling these requirements fully: neural networks frequently hallucinate or fail to retrieve information, and existing formalisms used by rules-based systems often struggle to produce flexible grammars with fluent outputs. This article proposes a hybrid architecture that integrates the capabilities of each to solve these specific limitations. This system functionally unites: (1) A rules-based content selection component grounded in "dataflow transduction," a novel formal framework. This mechanism leverages declarative rules applied to an agent's data processing graphs to construct context-free grammars defining contextually viable response options. These generated grammatics then (2) guide a subsequent restricted decoding method used by a neural language generator, ensuring the output remains both fluid and adherent. Evaluation results based on human feedback demonstrate that this integrated design performs more favorably regarding relevance, fluency, and factual accuracy in comparison with purely neural or purely rules-based systems.

Our research identifies a previously unrecognized pattern called mixed confounded missingness (MCM). In MCM situations, a subset of missingness values depends on whether treatment was selected, while other values depend on the treatment itself.

We demonstrate that applying blind imputation strategies leads to models that perform inadequately; this imputation inadvertently strips away the specific information required for bias-free calculations and produces estimates. On the other hand, refusing any imputation also yields biased results, because treatment-driven patterns in missingness fragment the dataset into subpopulations, all yielding skewed averages at different scales. Our proposed remedy is "selective imputation": leveraging MCM insights to determine exactly which variables require completion and which do not. Empirical analysis confirms that applying selective data recovery techniques significantly improves various learners beyond other solutions for managing gaps in data.

This study investigates semantic correspondence estimation by leveraging unsupervised learning techniques. We comprehensively assess various recently proposed unsupervised methods across multiple difficult datasets, employing a unified evaluation protocol that varies elements such as backbone architectures, pre-training strategies, and the datasets used for pre-training and finetuning. To better analyze the failure modes of these approaches and illuminate a directive path for improvement, the proposed new framework of diagnosis is coupled along with a novel performance indicator which better aligns to the requirements of the matching process. To wrap up this thesis, a novel approach with respect to unsupervised correspondence estimation which utilizes the benefit of available pretrained features to facilitate optimal alignment occurs, resulting ultimately with a significant improvement over existing current techniques with respect to performance results.

For annotating words in a historical document archive to support image recognition requires both time and experts in fields like history or paleography. Furthermore, acquiring example images for an exhaustive lexicon of all words is impractical in real-life applications. To recognize novel or lexicon-out-of-vocabulary characters under these constraints, Zero-shot learning proves highly suitable. Extending the best-performing Zero-shot word recognition approach, Pho(SC)Net, we introduce a CTC-enabled Hybrid Model (Pho(SC)-CTC). This architecture integrates Phocs features extracted by Pho(SC) with the connectionist temporal classification framework for the ultimate classification. We achieved favorable results when evaluating the system on two historical document datasets and an artificial handwritten set, substantating the effectiveness of both the hybrid Pho(SC)-CTC model and Pho(SC)Net.

While deeplearning can streamline numerous clinically valuable image-analysis tasks, its integration into practice has faced obstacles due to reduced transparency and explainability in advanced algorithms relative to traditional statistical approaches. A critical limitation involves the insufficient use of reliable methods for conveying prediction uncertainty in many clinical deeplearning models, thereby constraining their practical adoption in complex medical decisions. Additionally, concerns driven by documented algorithmic bias have increased skepticism regarding their deployment in clinical settings. This study investigates how conformal prediction acts as a supportive tool, enhancing existing models by offering an intuitively understandable framework for uncertainty that aligns better with clinician transparency expectations. By conducting interviews to explore practical interests, specific clinical scenarios have been designed. These were tested via multiple conformalcon prediction approaches on skin lesion data. The research also details modifications to this prediction logic to ensure fair adaptation across diverse skin tones using techniques for equalized coverage and compares the results against other measures of epistemic uncertainty.

This work investigates efficient methods for obtaining exact samples from a discrete distribution $\mathcal{D}$ using only access to comparisons between its support elements. Specifically, assuming we receive data in the form of pairs $(x, S)$—where $S$, drawn from a set distribution $\mathcal{Q}$, identifies the participants, and $x$, drawn from the conditional distribution $\mathcal{D}_S$, indicates the loser or winner (here interpreted as a participant involved in the win)—our goal is to generate a clean output sample $y$ adhering strictly to the true distribution $\mathcal{D}$. Our primary focus concerns comparisons where the support set $S$ always contains exactly two elements. We introduce a Markov chain stationary at $\mathcal{D}$ with a sampling algorithm based on Coupling from the Past. Nevertheless, this method's sample complexity varies with the specific structure of $\mathcal{D}$, remaining prohibitively high in some natural instances. The central contribution of our study is an efficient exact sampler with complexity decoupled from $\mathcal{D}$. We achieve this by designing a parametrized Markov chain that utilizes a strong learning algorithm from pairwise comparisons (Shah et al. and MLR 2nd, 7, 2) to approximate its target stationary distribution much more effectively, relying only on an approximate distribution instead. This approach for accelerating Markov chain mixing when driven by a probabilistically close distribution is both universally applicable and theoretically distinct.

Single-subject prediction of brain disorders using neuroimaging has garnered significant recent interest. However, prediction model accuracy on extensive multi-site datasets struggles notably with certain heterogeneous conditions, specifically Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), remaining unsatisfactory. This study introduces a novel two-stage architecture to enhance the diagnosis of diverse psychiatric conditions by leveraging resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI). Initially, we implement a self-supervised mask completion protocol trained on healthy participant data, effectively capitalizing on distinctions between healthy controls and clinical cases. Secondly, discriminative feature representations extracted from this stage are utilized to train a supervised classification algorithm. To accommodate rs-fMRI data structures, we have formulated Graph-S4, an iterative refinement extending the state-space S4 model graph architectures where exact structural relationships are pre-unspecified. Our results indicate that synergizing this two-stage framework with the Graph-S4 architecture substantially boosts the efficacy of single-subject diagnostic predictive systems for both ASD and MDD across three separate, publicly available, multi-institutional clinical cohorts featuring large volumes of rs-fMRI data.

Although combinatorial formulas describing the true inverse for matrices with odd cycles were previously established, this study introduces a combinatorial formula for the Moore-Penrose inverse concerning matrices with even cycles, thereby addressing a longstanding unsolved challenge.

In recent years, there has been a growing focus on establishing partnerships between celebrities using their faces and voices by harnessing YouTube's audio-video data. Previous studies utilized metric learning techniques to construct an embedddding space conducive to matching and recognition tasks. However, despite minor advancements, these approaches are limiting due to their reliance on distance-based margin parameters, suboptimal runtime training efficiency, and the need for meticulously designed negative mining strategies. This paper argues that achieving a discriminative joint feature space for linking facial identities with voices depends on creating enriched representations alongside a robust, yet computationally economical, training signal. To this purpose, we introduce a lightweight, modular mechanism that integrates complementary signals from both audio and video domains to produce enriched fused embeddings, subsequently grouping these by identity using orthogonality rules. We designate this proposed strategy as "Fusion and Orthogonal Projection" (FOP) and deploy it within a dual-stream architecture, demonstrating its effectiveness across a range of evaluations on the VoxCeleb1 and MAV-Celeb datasets, including cross-modal verification and matching. Empirical results demonstrate superior performance relative to state-of-the-art basels and highlight how the new supervisory formulation offers greater efficiency. Additionally, this framework examines the role of multi-country support through voice-visual comparisons across several languages. The source code is publicly accessible at: \url{

Stabbing queries over interval collections are conventionally resolved using segment trees. A dynamic iteration of the segment tree, implemented by van Kreveld and Overmars, employs red-black trees for its rebalancing mechanisms. This research introduces zipped segment trees—dynamic segment structures derived from zip trees initially presented by Tarjan et al. In order to maintain necessary segment tree invariants during the zip tree process, we develop appropriate protocols to uphold these properties by utilizing these operations to manage memory allocation during insertion and other tasks. Experimental performance and evaluation of the new sorting trees reveals that the sorted trees outperform the alternatives that use rotations as their basis.

Hand gestures constitute valuable tools in the field of human-computer interaction (HCI) with broad applications including robotic surgery and sign language interpretation. A primary difficulty in recognizing these gestures lies in the diverse shapes and sizes of hands, making reliable detection and trajectory tracking challenging. Consequently, developing a tracking method that succeeds across varying hand characteristics is a core objective. To address this, a motion template driven by optical flow (designated as OFMT) is introduced; OFMT serves as a compact, single-image encoding of the kinetic data inherent to a gesture. Experimental validation using bare hands with open or closed palms and also when worn under green gloves demonstrates the generation of high-precision OFMT images across these varied conditions. While recent advancements have favored the substantial improvements of deep network techniques over legacy hand-crafted feature methods, combining multiple data streams often further optimizes recognition accuracy in the literature. Aligning with these findings, this study presents an efficient yet concise optical flow-based motion template and a two-stream fusion architecture specifically for gesture recognition. Fused layers feature two distinct networks: a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (C3D) for spatiotemporal understanding using gesture videos, complemented by a 2D Convolutional Neural Network that processes OFMT images. While C3D models the video effectively, OFMT contributes supplementary motion nuances while filtering out extraneous gestures. Despite their individual utility, merging these streams through a fusion mechanism amplifies the reliability of the outcomes. Final validation confirms the robustness and utility of this proposed two-stream framework, validated performance across two distinct database collections.
