We investigate the $^{13}\text{Be}$ structure through a kine-matically full (p, pn) experiment conducted in inverse kinematics at 265 MeV per nucleon. Our analysis compares the measured $^{13}\text{Be}$ relative-energy spectrum against "Transfer-to-the-Continuum" calculations, utilizing overlaps between the $^{14}\text{Be}$ ground-state wave function (calculated from models that assume $^{13}\text{Be}{\rm n}$ structure consists of just two-body motion outside the core). Finally, we discuss how single-neutrino $1p$ or $1d$ continuum states need to be treated to best fit and interpret the low-energy features of the resulting spectra.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have attained remarkable success across various graph-learning tasks by synergizing node features with network topologies. Contemporary GNNs rely on iterative message-passing mechanisms to aggregate features from neighbors or proximal nodes. However, their efficacy is often strictly constrained by global assortativity—the phenomenon where nodes connect based on similar attributes. In reality, many graphs display diverse or heterogeneous connection patterns, rendering the traditional global assortativity coefficient an inadequate metric for quantifying such mixing and predicting GNN learnability. To address this, we introduce "node-level assortativity," a finer-grained approach that better captures local mixing heterogeneity and aligns with model performance. Our findings demonstrate a high correlation between GNN efficacy and node-level assortativity. To surpass these limitations, we propose transforming input graphs into computation graphs that distinctly separate edges representing structural relationships from those representing feature proximities. This multi-relational computation graph exhibits enhanced overall assortativity while retaining rich semantic information. By evaluating GNNs on this transformed structure and dynamically choosing between utilizing structural or proximity information depending on the graph's mixing pattern, we achieve performance gains across varied scenarios. Empirical evaluations confirm the effectiveness of this proposed transformation framework in boosting results for semi-supervised node classification across multiple real-world benchmarks.

We propose a unified framework analyzing metric and scalar perturbations throughout various energy scales within scalar-tensor gravity. This is achieved via two linked patterns of symmetry-breaking: one stemming from the field's non-trivial vacuum expectation values and another arising from the distinction between the background fields and those forming perturbations. We demonstrate that the geometric optics approximation, typically employed to separate high-frequency components, fails for such perturbations as gauge transformations intertwine different orders of the tensor and scalar sectors. Consequently, we derive the equations of motion characterizing these perturbations and analyze their behavior at low and high frequencies. Finally, we apply this phenomenology to screening mechanisms—specifically chameleon and symmetron—proving that scalar waves remain concealed across all frequencies and are thus undetectable.

We demonstrate that the tree-level S-matrices within superstring field theories formulated via homotopy-algebra structures align perfectly with results from the first-quantized approach. We present a comprehensive proof specifically for heterotic string field theory, showing that extending this framework to type II and open superstring field theories follows logically from there without difficulty.

In the dense environment surrounding supernovae, flavor evolution is driven rapid oscillations due to the significant interactions between neutrinos. Recent progress indicates that expanding from the traditional three-flavor framework to a comprehensive six-species model alters both the conditions for and the results of these processes. This work extends earlier research in this area, conducting full space-and-time numerical simulations based on six neutrino species. The outcomes demonstrate that our previous findings hold up under qualitative scrutiny in these extended evolutionary dynamics. These results reinforce the conclusion that investigating fast flavor conversions requires moving beyond the simplified restriction to just three flavor species.

Users regulate high-frequency dissipative behavior within a linear spectrum through adjustments to algorithmic parameters. An analytical investigation into the spectral properties indicates that the stability requirements (the CFL condition), as well as stability regions, remain constant despite increase in the accuracy order while the stiffness matrix. Additionally, optimized preconditioners are adapted effectively to use the general spectrum for $\gamma$-type discretization of isogeo-rectilinear matrices when using diagonal-scaled, univariate, and parametric mass matrix. They feature impressive performances robust to varying mesh size and B-spline degree. Furthermore, these decomposable matrices are more computationally expensive than the fully assembled ones. Our resulting algorithms need a minor addition to existing implementations of $\gamma$-type schemes. Additionally, the performance and versatility of this scheme is illustrated on both single-element patches of isogeo-rectilinear meshes and multi-element test cases.

To accommodate intricate search scenarios characterized by complex and fluid information needs that shift over time, search systems must dynamically adjust how they present results. An effective strategy for this involves leveraging both historical user feedback and content context to continuously refine rankings for dynamic searching. Researchers have proposed Roliark, a reinforcement learning-enabled system designed for this purpose. The approach establishes an adapted reinforcement learning structure to encapsulate core components of dynamic search operations and employs a unique learning-to-rank model within subsequent iterations. This recurrent model leverages a Neural network with Long Short Term Memory units (LSTM) across previous documents. It predicts the potential benefit of ranking each subsequent item while drawing from the ranking history. Furthermore, user feedback integration is managed through an LSTM-based variation of Rocchio's algorithm. Together, these advancements enable RL-Track to surpass previous techniques performed in TREC's 2017 Dynamic Track and to outperform all methods deployed in the 2016 TREC Domain segments, after applying modifications to the state-of-the-art.

Acquiring meaningful representations is fundamental to the triumph of contemporary machine learning. At present, representation learning predominantly operates by embedding data within Euclidean space. Yet, emerging research indicates that non-Euclidean metric spaces often offer a superior model for specific domains, suggesting that a poor geometric choice can degrade performance. This study seeks to remove inductive biases inherent in the geometry of traditional embedding spaces. Specifically, we introduce a framework mapping data to broader non-vector metric spaces, defined here as a weighted graph equipped with a shortest path distance. Structured in this manner, graphs possess the capacity to accommodate an infinite variety of geometries through appropriate adjustments to their edge and weight configurations. Our primary contribution is the proposal of PRODIGE, a technique capable of learning a point-cloud weighted graph via end-to-end gradient descent. Due to their enhanced adaptability and reduced reliance on restrictive model assumptions, PRODIGE demonstrates superior capability compared to standard embedding-based methodologies. Empirical results across numerous tasks, encompassing classification, compression, and recommender system problems like collaborative filtering, validate the outstanding efficacy of this approach.

Three-dimensional (3D) multi-object tracking serves as a fundamental pillar within the perception framework of autonomous vehicles, enabling essential capabilities like obstacle avoidance and trajectory planning. While these vehicles increasingly rely on multiple sensor types to enhance precision, current tracking approaches often depend solely on one data source or fail to leverage the complementary information from diverse sensors, despite the prominence of sensor fusion in detection networks. This study introduces an end-to-end network for synchronized object detection and tracking via radar-camera fusion. We implemented a center-centric fusion technique for detection and employed a greedy strategy for track association, which leverages depth, velocity, and two-dimensional displacement data to correlate detections over time. By integrating these dimensions, the tracker demonstrates exceptional robustness against object occlusion and overlap, effectively distinguishing between them using velocity and depth cues. Validated on the challenging nuScenes benchmark, the method achieved an AMOTA score of 20.0, surpassing existing camera-based solutions as well as the baseline LiDAR approach. Furthermore, its online capability with a processing time of 35 ms per frame makes it highly practical for real-time autonomous driving deployment and is available for non-daily, non-profit research on GitHub at `107070603`. This solution provides an efficient route toward accurate and reliable autonomous navigation.

Intelligence and Sensing (IS) stands out as a pivotal technology for future wireless networks. It leverages wireless resource sharing to achieve superior performance compared to standalone S&C architectures, and quantifying their tradeoff forms the theoretical cornerstone of the IS conceptuality. This paper examines a vector-channel point-to-point IS model, proposing to utilize S&C performance as the foundational tool for illustrating S&C compromises. Specifically, we investigate the scenario wherein waveform signals from a single transmitter carrying out S&I activities simultaneously reach two separate ISs. Performing S&I at the same time necessitates a structured IS, ideally using a code sequence that represents data at the source and destination, functioning also as standard IS in other scenarios. Bayesian experimental design (BED) seeks to create experiments optimized for information gathering from collected data, typically by maximizing the mutual information (MI) between that data and the underlying model parameters. However, exact analytical computation of MI is often impossible for implicit models featuring intractable data distributions; in such cases, recent methods utilize neural networks with lower-bound estimators optimized via gradient ascent. A limitation found in prior work, specifically by Kleinegesse et al., is the dependence of gradient computation on accessible sampling paths for the lower-bound MI with respect to design variables—a requirement that often fails for implicit models. This work addresses that hurdle with a hybrid gradient approach that integrates advancements in variational MI estimation, Evolution Strategies, and Black-box Stochastic Gradient Ascent (SGA) to maximize the lower-bound MI without relying on sampling path gradients. Experiments reveal that this unified, scalable procedure significantly enhances the practicality of applying Bayesian Experimental Design across high-dimensional designspaces involving implicit models.

We introduce Poly-GAN, a new conditional Generative Adversarial Network designed initially for the task of placing clothing onto humans in poses that differ by angle, a problem known in the fashion industry. Poly-GAN conditions on inputs, making it applicable across various tasks such as seamless image blending, splicing, and inpainting. Most current techniques follow a three-stage workflow where distinct networks are dedicated sequentially to misalignment correction, blending the aligned garment into the model image, and refining the final output. Poly-GAN stands as the only solution to date using a single, unified architecture to execute all three of these operations. By applying conditionals at every layer within the network and employing skip links between matching encoder states and their corresponding decoders, our design achieves these capabilities. The system can geometrically manipulate the garment relative to the model using color information and bone structure. Additionally, regardless of how clothing is rotated, Poly-GAN can handle fine-scale blending and automatic mask repair for uneven holes within garments. By employing two different metrics (Structural Similarity and Inception Score indices) for the DeepFashion dataset we have obtained experiment the best state of art results.

N-ImageNet is a large-scale dataset introduced to support robust, fine-grained object recognition specifically designed for event cameras. Constructed using programmable hardware, the data collection process involved an event camera systematically scanning images of multiple datasets. This resource serves as a rigorous benchmark due to its extensive variety of classes and numerous samples; empirical results confirm that pre-training on N-ImageNet boosts the performance of event-based classifiers and enables training with limited labeled data. Furthermore, we offer multiple N-ImageNet variants to assess classifier stability under different camera motion and adverse light conditions, while proposing a new event representation method to mitigate performance drops. This appears to be the initial quantitative study addressing how diverse environmental factors impact event-based recognition. Finally, N-ImageNet, alongside our variants, aims to inform realistic applications of event-based recognition systems in practical settings.

Dense video captioning involves identifying distinct events within untrimmed videos and generating text descriptions for each occurrence. While previous approaches rely predominantly on visual data and overlook audio, humans heavily depend on sound and specific speech to comprehend surroundings. Consequently, we propose a novel framework for dense video captioning designed to leverage multiple input modalities, with an emphasis on the enhancements offered by audio and spoken word signals. To this end, we employ an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system to derive temporally synced textual transcripts which function similarly to subtitles. These transcripts, along with video frames and the audio waveform itself, serve as distinct parallel inputs. Additionally, we cast the captioning task as a machine translation problem, employing the advanced Transformer model to transform these heterogeneous multi-modal inputs into textual outputs. Our approach is validated on the ActivityNet Captions dataset; ablation results confirm that auditory components contribute significant value to audio-conditional dense video captioning, highlighting their complementary nature. Moreover, we offer a detailed evaluation by incorporating original YouTube category metadata into an analysis of the ActivityNet results. Source code and resources are accessible on our public repository.

Detecting the position taken in a news body regarding a headline is the initial prerequisite for automated fake news detection; this research addresses that stance identification using a two-stage ensemble model. By inputting hand-crafted features solely into a gradient boosting classifier for this classification task, our method achieved a score of 114.86 (representing 80.80%) for the first category. We present multi-camera trajectory forecasting (MCTF), a challenge involving the prediction of an entity's path across a camera network. Despite the prevalence of multi-camera systems in fields like traffic monitoring and surveillance, current forecasting techniques predominantly rely on single-camera setups (SCTF), restricting their validity for these complex applications. Additionally, the constrained field-of-view seen through a solitary lens makes long-term prediction infeasible. We mitigate SCTF limitations by proposing an MCTF framework that integrates relative location estimates from diverse perspectives to forecast an object’s future positions in all potential views. Operating under a "Which-When-Where" paradigm, our method predicts specific camera visibility, temporal occurrence, and localized coordinates of objects. Central to this effort is our introduction of "trajectory tensors"—a novel encoding mechanism for multi-view trajectories and their uncertainty. We construct and evaluate various encoder-decoder architectures designed for these tensors using a dedicated dataset of 1,355 minutes of video captured across 120 distinct camera viewpoints within our custom MCTF repository [46]. Empirical results demonstrate significant improvements over existing coordinate-based MCTF approaches and SCTF methods adapted for multi-camera scenarios. Accessible implementation and resources are hosted at: github.com/olly-styles/Trajectory-Tensors.

Future cosmic weak lensing studies promise measurements of cosmological parameters with extraordinary precision. To prepare, extensive simulations featuring realistic populations of galaxies must validate analysis pipelines; however, existing high-volume, high-resolution models often incur prohibitive computational costs, making the task intractable. We address the challenge of generating emulations of 3D galaxy orientations by proposing Deep Generative Modeling. Specifically, we have engineered a new Diffusion model based on score functions, optimized for operation across the $SO(3)$ manifold. As a result, the model successfully captures the correlated alignments of galaxies and dark matter halos, producing outputs that strictly match those found in high-fidelity hydrodynamic reference simulations from a statistical standpoint.

This publication serves as the foundation paper for the accepted "One-Minute Gradual-Emotion Recognition" (OMG-Emotion) challenge at IJCNN, aiming to advance long-duration emotion classification through neural networks, benefiting the broader IJCNN community. The novel aspect of our proposed corpus lies in our unique data acquisition and annotation strategy, designed to capture emotion expressions developing within specific temporal contexts. Unlike other datasets, our corpus is the only one of its kind offering multimodal gradual annotations focused explicitly on contextual emotional shifts. The data were collected via a meticulously curated YouTube video selection defined by specific search queries and filtering, ensuring that every instance demonstrates an organic, continuous progression of emotion over time. To ensure fairness and standardization for evaluating various recurrent and convolution neural networks, a complete experimental protocol and multiple unimodal baseline runs have been provided.

Can both discriminative and generative capabilities be unified within a single neural network? This question has recently received a positive resolution through Joint Energy-based Models (JEM), which have demonstrated simultaneous excellence in image classification accuracy and generation quality. However, despite these recent strides, JEM still faces two significant hurdles: a classification accuracy gap relative to standard softmax classifiers and a generational quality lag behind state-of-the-art deep generative models. To address this, we introduce several novel training strategies aimed at narrowing both performance deficiencies. First, we integrate Sharpened Awareness-Minimization (SAM), a recently proposed framework designed to enhance the smoothness of the energy landscape in JEM, thereby bolstering generalization. Second, we omit data augmentation from the maximum likelihood estimation process within JEM, effectively reducing its adverse effect on image synthesis. Comprehensive experiments conducted across multiple datasets reveal that the resulting SADA-RM model attains state-of-the-art results and substantially surpasses baseline JEM methods in image classification, image generation, probability calibration, out-of-distribution detection, and adversarial robustness.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have established themselves as superior methods for image classification; however, their high computational demand and memory usage make them impractical for resource-constrained embedded devices. While quantization is a common technique to reduce complexity and memory at the expense of accuracy, we propose a novel approach to optimally quantize weights, biases, and activations layer by layer while strictly controlling accuracy degradation for efficient inference specifically tailored to these devices. Our method converts high-precision 32-bit floating-point values into low-bitwidth fixed points by optimally determining bitwidths and fractional offsets for each layer of a pre-trained network without requiring re-training. Crucially, unlike methods that optimize parameters in isolation and suffer up to 50% accuracy losses, we consider the interdependence of all quantization errors across parameters. Consequently, we achieve a reduction to low precision with accuracy losses of under 1%. Compared to commercial tools that force uniform 8-bit precision, the proposed method reduces memory consumption by 53.0% on average and cutting multiplication costs at 77.5%. We attribute this success to our adoption of layer-wise quantization.

This study examines the optimal placement of relief goods for logistics planning ahead of a projected hurricane landfall. The issue is formulated as a multiperiod network flow optimization aimed at minimizing operational logistics expenses and the costs associated with unmet demand. Assistance demand, which shifts in step with a Markov process, is predicted based on the storm's anticipated strength and projected landing zone, adjusted by when the storm is expected to occur. The research encompasses two specific contexts: fixed, known landfall times versus stochastic landfall instances. For fixed landfalls, we present a completely adaptive, multi-stage stochastic programming (MSP) framework enabling planners to update their distribution plans sequentially as new hurricane data emerges. For stochastic landfalls, we adapt a prior model (Guigues, 2021), accommodating stage-depency. We evaluate these strategies against static and rolling-horizon, two-stage stochastic approaches. The numerical simulations highlight significant operational benefits derived from using full adaptive MSP models for emergency logistical efforts.

Primordial black holes (PBHs), which may constitute dark matter across a vast mass range, are expected to emit significant fluxes of energetic (∼10 MeV) neutrinos if their masses fall within $10^{15}–10^{17}$ grams, a mechanism known as Hawking radiation evaporation. We investigate the feasibility of identifying light, non-rotating PBHs using next-generation neutrino detectors, specifically focusing on the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) and THeIA. By modeling anticipated event spectra for various PBH masses and spin values across these two facilities, we determine their expected 95% confidence level constraints. Our findings indicate that DUNE and THeIA can establish robust, competitive limits on PBH dark matter, thereby probing regions of parameter space largely unyielded by current gamma-ray searches.

Pulsar Timing Arrays are anticipated to detect gravitational waves from supermassive black hole binaries in eccentric inspiraling configurations. We evaluate the computational efficiencies of four calculation strategies for relativistic SMBHB signals: approximations, Fourier expansions, post-circular expansions, and numerical integration. Our analysis indicates that using the approximate analytic expressions yields the fastest performance, achieving roughly a fifty-fold speedup compared to other approaches. Knowledge representation learning (KRL) has recently become the leading approach for handling queries on knowledge graphs (KGs). By embedding both KG entities and the queries themselves, this method positions entities that serve as answers in close proximity within the latent dimension spaces. However, despite extensive KRL research, current studies predominantly address either uniform knowledge graphs or completion tasks focused on inferring missing facts. Consequently, tackling complex logical questions regarding multi-faceted KGs remains unresolved. To address this limitation, we introduce ROMA, an innovative KRL framework designed specifically for resolving logical queries across multi-view KGs. The system differentiates itself in four critical areas. First, it structures multi-view KGs as an overlay of distinct sub-KGs representing individual views, thereby accommodating numerous KG variants previously studied, such as temporal graphs. Second, it handles sophisticated logical queries incorporating dynamic constraints on relations and data viewpoints, capable of managing complex topologies or multi-source perspectives. Third, it maintains high scalability even when processing knowledge graphs comprising millions of entities across dozens of fine-grained views. Fourth, it generalizes effectively to query patterns and observation types not encountered during training. Comprehensive experiments using real-world knowledge graph datasets confirm that ROMA consistently outperforms alternative approaches.

The researcher analyzed several simple cases regarding different particle detectors to prove why one must properly account coordinate transformation problems when using such techniques.

Standard domain adaptation techniques often fail when significant discrepancies separate the source and target domains. Gradual domain adaptation offers a potential remedy by utilizing an intermediate distribution to smoothly interpolate from the source to the target. Existing methods rely on assumptions that many close-knit intermediate domains exist, making self-training with unlabeled data feasible. In practice, however, the number of available intermediate domains is often limited, and the gap between adjacent ones can be too large, causing traditional gradual self-training protocols to fail. To address these challenges within an unsupervised framework, we propose employing normalizing flows to synthesize pseudo-intermediate domains, which subsequently drive the gradual adaptation process. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach successfully overcomes prior constraints while enhancing classification accuracy.

This study introduces a novel greedy algorithm for sparse approximation, designated as Single L_1 Selection (SLS). The method operates via a greedy forward approach in which each new component is chosen by solving an optimization task combining a least-squares objective penalized against the L_1 norm of remaining variables, ultimately selecting the component with the highest amplitude on this criterion. Experimental validation using challenging sparse deconvolution cases with highly correlated dictionaries demonstrates that SLS outperforms widely used greedy methods, as well as Basis Pursuit Denoising, specifically in sparse scenarios.

**Results:** We present Peptipedia, an intuitive online tool designed for searching, characterizing, and analyzing peptide sequences that aggregates data from thirty prior databases, establishing it as the most comprehensive repository for peptide activity records currently available. Burgers' equation serves as a widely examined model in applied mathematics, exhibiting significant links to one-dimensional Navier-Stokes flows and vehicular dynamics, among others. Extending earlier studies, we investigate solutions within the complex plane, specifically examining the behavior of complex singularities and how the locations of these points influence solutions along the real axis. For an initial scenario featuring a simple pole in both the upper and lower halves, we employ formal asymptotics for both small and large time scales to define early- and late-time dynamics, noting that infinitely many new singularities are born instantly at $t=0$. In this small-time inner region, these emerging points align increasingly along anti-Stokes lines, while the analysis also indicates whether the singularity nearest to the real axis migrates closer or further. For intermediate time frames, we combine the exact solution, the method of steepest descents, and AAA (Adaptive Antecedence Approximated) techniques to chart the singularities' paths. Furthermore, we link the trajectory of the singularity closest to the real axis to gradients in real-valued steepening solutions. Despite the existence of a closed-form solution for Burgers' equation, we intentionally utilize an eclectic combination of analytical approaches, aiming to establish a computational strategy applicable to other nonlinear PDEs lacking exact solutions.

This research examines the efficacy of applying Deep Learning (DL) methods to classify planetary nebulae (PNe), emphasizing the distinction between true PNe and other celestial objects alongside morphological categorization. Leveraging three ImageNet-pre-trained architectures via a deep transfer learning framework, the study utilizes image datasets from the HASH database and Pan-STARRS. Specifically, DenseNet201 emerged as the top performer among the evaluated algorithms. While morphological classification for distinct structural types, Bipolar, Elliptical, and Round showed success in identifying roughly half of instances within these groups, expanding this efficacy appears to depend on additional data or training enhancements. While similarity or homophily often accounts for patterns like transitivity and triangle density in complex networks, phenomena ranging from labor division to protein-protein interactions frequently arise via complementarity (differences and synergies). This study demonstrates a connection between complementarity and the prevalence of quadrangles (4-cycles) and bipartite-like dense subgraphs. We associate both principles with their signature motifs and define two families of metrics: (1) structural similarity coefficients, which generalize local clustering measures and capture the entire spectrum of similarity-driven structures; and (2) structural complementarity coefficients defined analogously but centered on quadrangles. Validation across social and biological networks reveals that these metrics effectively capture domain-specific structural properties. They enable the distinction between different types of social relations and quantify growing structural diversity in protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks throughout the tree of life. We argue that complementation may offer more accurate explanations than homophily for certain relational types, while also holding utility for enhancing current link prediction techniques. Additionally, we provide a Python package containing efficient algorithms to compute these coefficients.

Recent advancements in implicit neural representations, notably NeRF, demonstrate significant capacity for compressively encoding high-fidelity scene and lighting data within compact networks. Nevertheless, real-time application remains hamstrung by the high computational burden of evaluating these networks repeatedly along viewing rays, often necessitating dozens of petaFLOPS. Our research bridges the gap between theory and practice, targeting real-time synthetic content for applications such as virtual reality and gaming. We establish that image quality can remain intact if ray sampling density is reduced by directing samples specifically toward occluded surface regions. To achieve this, we introduce a depth oracle network capable of predicting optimal ray sampling locations through just one neural evaluation. Crucially, our approach utilizes a classification network operating on logarithmically split and spherically warped depths to accurately localize surfaces rather than merely approximating depth maps. Combining these elements yields DONeRF, our dual-network architecture featuring a depth oracle pre-steps evaluation followed by localized shading sampling. Relative to standard NeRF with known depth priors, our method achieves up to 48-fold inference speedup. Uniquely, unlike other concurrent ray-marching optimizations, our approach imposes no extra memory overhead for acceleration structures or caching. Consequently, our solution achieves interactive rendering speeds of 20 FPS on a single graphics unit.

Although reinforcement learning offers immense potential for advanced autonomous driving, existing RL approaches struggle with low data efficiency and training oscillation when dealing with high-dimensional tasks. This paper introduces "Learn to Drive with Virtual Memory" (LVM), an algorithm designed to resolve these issues by condensing high-dimensional inputs into concise latent states and learning a latent dynamic model to capture the agent's experiences. This model generates imagined latent trajectories that constitute a form of virtual memory. By propagating gradients from an imagined set of these latent trajectories through the learned model to train the policy, LVM achieves greater data efficiency in an implicit off-line algorithm for planning and evaluating near-optimal behavior. Additionally, a double-critic structure has been developed to handle distribution shifts that cause divergence from optimal trajectories, providing further training guarantees for learning policies and improving robustness. Ultimately, in the context of visual self-driven systems with either stochastic inputs or standard images, this approach can utilize limited samples for planning and evaluation more effectively while maintaining accuracy.

Modeling the transport of sediments remains a difficult yet critical task for understanding particulate geophysical fluids. This study investigates sediment transport within the collisional regime, specifically emphasizing a continuum-based granular flow model. To achieve this, a hybrid method was developed that integrates a Coulomb model representing friction with the kinetic theory of granular gases. This new framework is derived by comparing results with coupled fluid-particle simulations against standard kinetic theories that previously failed in this area. While developing this improved model, a fluctuating energy balance was calculated in discrete simulations for systematic validation against kinetic theory closures. Analysis revealed that particle friction influences the radial distribution function and heightens energy dissipation, confirming findings from prior literature. Additionally, due to the presence of saltating (bouncing) particles, which are not accounted for in traditional kinetic theory, discrepancies in viscosity and diffusivity were observed, particularly in dilute zones of the granular flow. The findings also demonstrated that a quadratic drag force significantly enhances granular energy dissipation based on fluctuating energy flux. Utilizing these insights, specific alterations to kinetic theory closures were proposed. Tests show that this modified model accurately simulates discrete behavior across the full depth of the granular flow, impacts their rheological properties, successfully recovers the ρ(I) rheological relationship in regimes allowing dense movement.

This paper introduces parameterized expressions for canal hypersurfaces defined as envelops generated by families of pseudo hyperspheres and pseudo hyperbolic hyperspheres within $E^4_1$, whose central trajectories follow pseudo null, partial null, or null curves. Several examples constructing these hypersurfaces are provided, followed by a presentation of specific characterizations for tubular hypersurfaces in $E^4_1$.

Specifically, average top-1 accuracy improvements of 1.35% and 0.48% were achieved respectively. These observations suggest that our biologically inspired residual designs offer superior generalized functionality and represent a viable trajectory for enhancing the discriminative power of existing state-of-the-art image classification systems.

This study investigates numerical discrepancies in large-eddy simulation (LES) for both wall-bounded turbulence and isotropic cases, utilizing an approach where the subgrid-scale (SGS) terms are derived from filtered direct-numerical simulation (DNS) data to aid LES. We demonstrate that this method exhibits zero error when the interaction between numerical differentiation operators and filters generates no commutation errors. Consequently, the technique enables the tracking of how numerical errors develop over time for different schemes at resolutions typical of LES. The results indicate that these numerical errors generally match the order of modeling errors, frequently counteracting one another; this suggests that relying solely on filtered DNS to train supervised machine learning for robust SGS models may be inadequate because such an approach overlooks cumulative numerical errors. While advanced machine learning models are vulnerable to data poisoning attacks aimed at compromising integrity, current research primarily relies on ad hoc techniques limited to specific model types and either restricted to binary classifiers or dependent on gradients. To remedy this gap, this paper introduces a novel, model-independent label-flipping attack that leverages data multimodality. The adversary targets class clusters under a label-flipping budget, and our approach achieves linear time complexity relative to dataset size; notably, it can double model error within the same budget. The authors further propose a robust defense utilizing the Synthetic Reduced Nearest Neighbor (SRNN) model, capable of detecting and excluding flipped samples during training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed attack severely degrades performance across various models, while the SRNN-based defense significantly surpasses other conventional methods in recovering accuracy against these sophisticated attacks.

To navigate challenges arising from singular formulations and unbounded kinetic energy, we develop a revised reduction technique. Furthermore, we establish numerous asymptotic properties for this system.

In 2020, Bang-Jensen et al. extended the concept of the Haj\'os join from graphs to directed graphs (digraphs), generalizing various vertex coloring results. Despite showing that many digraphs can be generated through directed Haj\'os joins followed by identifying independent vertices, the task of reconstructing the precise sequence of operations remains computationally difficult. Consequently, Bang-Jensen et al. formulated a problem finding the Haj\'os solution for constructing the symmetric 5-cycle from a complete symmetric digraph with order 3. This problem has successfully been solved through a rank-based genetic algorithm enhanced with novel recombination and mutation operators derived from graph theory. In this approach, the Haj\'os Join served as recombination and vertex independence identification acted as mutation. Utilizing these methods yielded the targeted five symmetric cycle via exactly sixteen Haj\'os operations.

Recent developments in optical coherence tomography (OCT) now permit noninvasive, high-resolution visualization of the microscopic layers of the human retina. Consequently, OCT has become a routine clinical procedure and a cornerstone of ophthalmological research. This imaging modality enables ophthalmologists to assess how diverse retinal and systemic conditions affect retinal architecture more accurately than ever before. Despite these advantages, detecting and analyzing minute, localized alterations within the substructures of the retina in the early stages of retinal disease remains difficult. This overview introduces new visual analytics methodologies that facilitate the interactive investigation of initial retinal defects in individual cases as well as comparative multi-patient analyses, including evaluations against normative benchmarks, automatic quantification of diagnostically critical features, and advanced measurements. Created in tandem with experts from a premier OCT device manufacturer and ophthalmological researchers, these methods dramatically decreased the time and labor necessary for analyzing broad spectral OCT data sets, thereby contributing to several groundbreaking discoveries published in biomedical literature.

Monocular depth estimation remains a foundational challenge in computer vision that has recently gained substantial interest. Approaches that recast this task as a classification-regression problem to enhance performance are emerging, where continuous depth values are derived by merging discrete bin predictions with probability distribution maps. This paper introduces **BinsFormer**, a novel framework optimized for classification-regression-based depth estimation. We concentrate on two pivotal elements: 1) producing adaptive, appropriate bins and 2) facilitating rich interaction between bin predictions and probability distribution maps. specifically, the framework utilizes a Transformer decoder reframed as a set-to-set direct prediction to generate these bins. Furthermore, a multi-scale decoder architecture is integrated to comprehensively model spatial geometric cues, enabling coarse-to-fine depth map estimation. We also propose auxiliary scenario-understanding queries, demonstrating that performing an environment classification task helps the model implicitly learn discriminative atmospheric context. Extensive evaluations across the KITTI, NYU, and SUN RGB-D datasets confirm that **BinsFormer** achieves state-of-the-art performance surpassing prior monocular depth estimation techniques with significant gaps. Both source code and pretrained models have been open-sourced at [https://github.com/zhyever/Monocular-Depth-Estimation-Toolbox](https://github.com/zhyever/Monocular-Depth-Estimation-Toolbox).

Identifying patterns within massive, interconnected datasets is fundamental for driving innovation in science and business. This research addresses stream subgraph matching, a capability vital for diverse fields such as cyber defense and network analysis, where specific application needs—like data granularity, stream characteristics, and match criteria—require tailored control parameters. Traditional subgraph matching architectures struggle to address these varying domain-specific challenges due to their rigid focus. In response, this paper introduces **Mnemonic**, a flexible framework featuring a high-level API that facilitates the creation of diverse subgraph matching solutions. Beyond customization, Mnemonic integrates essential data management tools and optimizations designed for the low-latency processing of long-running, high-speed graph streams involving multiple relationships. Experiments confirm the system's robustness and adaptability, revealing it surpasses several leading approaches with speed improvements reaching up to a hundredfold.

This article introduces a novel 12-week Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) in Natural Language Processing (NLP), designed for non-English-speaking learners. Each week includes lectures, practical exercises, and quizzes, while three weeks feature Kaggle-format coding assignments. The course serves three key objectives: familiarizing students with fundamental NLP principles like language modeling, sequence and token embeddings, and the foundations of transformer preprocessing; introducing architectural solutions for in-demand real-world applications; cultivating practical text-processing abilities in multiple languages. Developed and recorded in 2020 for launch later that decade, early 2021 feedback indicates initial success.

Recent years have witnessed dramatic oil price fluctuation, causing conventional forecasting models to become ineffective. The primary reason for this failure lies in their focus on actual parameter values rather than their expected counterparts. This research proposes a systems dynamics framework integrated with expectation variables to determine oil prices. In our approach, price movements result from the interplay between expected and actual demand and supply. The foundation of our model comprises regression analysis of multiple historical time series datasets; subsequently, the model refinement involved adding relevant causal loops specific to the oil marketplace. We tested our system by simulating various historical scenarios. The resulting simulations align consistently with the observed historical trends of each tested scenario.

Social media platforms often face criticism for directing users down ideological "rabbit holes." However, earlier findings on the consistency of algorithmic radicalization have been conflicting, and existing research lacks structured methods to reduce this bias within recommendation engines. We undertook a systematic audit of YouTube's system, utilizing 100,000 deceptive proxy accounts to investigate three key issues: the presence of ideological bias, the magnitude of its growth, whether it constitutes self-reinforcing escalation (radicalization), and whether it progresses to extremism. We then designed and tested a grassroots intervention capable of reducing these biases without requiring YouTube's collaboration. Our results confirm that YouTube's algorithms, particularly for right-leaning users, indeed steer them toward increasingly biased and extreme content across both the home page and "up next" suggestions. Conversely, our proposed method effectively counters these biases by promoting a diverse and ideologically balanced feed. However, mitigating bias for right-leaning users proves more challenging than for others. Overall, while our assessment confirms YouTube drives users down ideological paths, the demonstrated intervention proves that these biases can be successfully mitigated.

Our research focuses on central-max-point tolerance graphs (central MPITGs) constructed by defining the points of standard MPTGs as the midpoints of corresponding intervals. Our analysis reveals that the class of these central MPTGs is equivalent to that of unit max-tolerance graphs. Furthermore, we demonstrate unit and proper variations of these graphs to be equivalent to both each other and proper interval graphs. Additionally, we present 50%-based variants: whereas for max-majority tolerance graphs, the class with 50% constraints differs from that of unit max-majority tolerance graphs, the relationship for minimum-majority tolerance graphs preserves class equality for both thresholds. This paper investigates spatiotemporal object-centric reasoning within video data. Our method prioritizes "object permanence"—capable of tracking object locations even during movement, occlusion, containment, or when being carried. While existing deep learning models frequently exhibit spatiotemporal biases in video reasoning contexts, we introduce Hopper, a system employing a Multi-hop Transformer to handle these permanence challenges. Hopper iteratively traverses image frames and object tracks, selectively skipping critical ones for given videos and spatial query inputs to infer final locations. To mitigate spatiotemporal biases, we utilize a contrastive loss during our experiments, testing performance on the CATER dataset. Our approach, running at 1 FPS jumps through essential frames to minimize computational load, reached 73.2% Top-1 accuracy. Furthermore, we established the CATER-h dataset to validate Hopper's ability to execute long-term, multi-step object localization tasks.

High-coherence laser sources in the visible to near-visible spectrum are essential for advanced positioning, navigation, and timing systems, alongside traditional and quantum sensing applications. Despite this importance, their laboratory-only deployment remains hindered by the considerable size and engineering complexity associated with currently developed benchtop lasers. We demonstrate a system-on-a-chip capable of generating these high-coherence, high-overt light waves by combining wavelength conversion and enhanced coherence via self-injection-locking into a single nonlinear resonator using this innovative methodology.

Verified in hybrid-integrated configurations, this simplified system achieves a remarkably low short-term spectral linewidth ranging from 10 to 30 kHz, delivering over 2 mW of optical power directly on the chip when frequency-converted. Additionally, heterogeneous integration techniques have demonstrated optical conversion efficiencies surpassing 25% at output levels exceeding 11 mW. The feasibility exists for cost-effective mass production by adapting this mature III-V silicon-compatible pump laser technology within thin-film lithium niobate platforms to standardize scalable production. Finally, because the coherence production mechanism relies on a transfer function rather than material specificity alone, it is applicable to other nonlinear interactions, such as optical parametric oscillation and various processes of frequency mixing and harmonic generation.

This research aims to introduce a mathematical framework to investigate drivers of wage disparity and explore its connections to consumption behavior and production technologies within an economy. By building a simplified heterodox model of an isolated market where consumption and production are distinct yet interconnected through tatonnement, the authors align their equilibrium outcomes with those of an equivalent Arrow-Debreu model. This approach identifies specific relational parameters that determine system equilibria and wages based on preferences. Furthermore, the paper details the formulation of consumer choice games where individual utilities act as strategies and wage levels serve as rewards, demonstrating through two examples that consumer choices expressed via adjusted utility functions can permeate the economy, influencing prices, production, and wages. Consequently, these consumer choices can effectively serve as a mechanism for redistributing wages.

Nevertheless, conventional techniques tend to either locate impulsion signals or validate features post-extraction. Generally, these standard methods lack efficiency and automate procedures, often failing to pinpoint crucial frequencies for vibration diagnostics. Consequently, irrelevant band data yields unnecessary analysis complexity. Addressing this, the current research introduces Band Relevance Factor (BRF). This novel approach utilizes spectral entropy for the automated selection of frequency bands vital for rotating machinery vibration analysis. Results are conveyed through relevance rankings and heatmap visual analysis. Validated across both synthetically and real-world data, BRF effectively identifies frequency bands containing essential information for such structural inspections.

Notably, at the percolation threshold under the percolation model of global hydrogen fraction, initial values are markedly increased for scenarios involving ionization starting internally. Complementary to percolation findings, we investigate the shape and morphology of expanding regions utilizing Shapefinders (SFs), defined as Minkowski functional ratios. This morphological distribution effectively identifies extreme models, such as the Clumped Comoving Density Model. Furthermore, in models excluding these extreme inclusions, only the length component of the shape changes during percolation; meanwhile, thickness and breadth maintain stability. This indicates a filamentous nature for ionization hydrogen at this transition state. Additionally, specific recombination factors contribute to a distinctive, cross-sectional morphology. In combination, these shape-based and statistical analyses yield valuable clues about the processes and characteristics of the Epoch of Hydrogen recombination period sources.

This study defines a tight connection among four distinct information theoretic issues: Campbelle source coding, Arikan's guessing, memoryless guessing by Huleihel and others, and the Bunte and Lapidoth order tasks partitioning challenge. First, we reveal their mathematical underpinnings through a general min-moment problem, yielding an optimum based on Renyi entropy. Next, we introduce the mismatched version of each issue within a unified framework and derive all corresponding asymptotic results accordingly. Moreover, we explore the ordered order tasks partitioning problem as an extension of Arikan's guessing challenge. Lastly, utilizing the developed unified approach and the framework established for the mismatch case of each issue, we demonstrate a mutual conversion between all the problems so that a known, optimum result within any single problem is efficiently applied toward all the other problems.

In this work, we observe the Hanbury Brown-Twiss effect within an ultra-cold bosonic mixture of $^{23}$Na$^{87}$Rb made feasible through a newly developed quantum microscope capable of imaging such molecules. We record density fluctuations displaying the hallmark bunching of the molecules as the 2D ensemble released from and later recaptured into an optical lattice demonstrates these correlations with 54% visibility and single-pair interference. The high-resolution microscope, which precisely locates every molecule with a resolution matching that of each individual lattice site, directly detects the spatial correlations purely from the molecules' quantum statistical properties; these findings lay the groundwork for future site-specific inquiries into interacting behaviors of molecular systems.

The study investigates, using nonlinear effects in a theoretical framework, phase transitions of binary fluids toward inhomogeneous states along a single spatial dimension. Results demonstrate that below the spinodal point, phase stratification emerges initially, followed, as conditions cool further past the zenith of such stratification, by a second-order transformation into a state characterized by phase concentration waves. Additionally, entropy and heat capacity values attributed to this spatial inhomogeneity are quantified, culminating in a temperature versus average concentration phase diagram.

> Reconfigurable metasurfaces promise significant advancements in photonics technology by merging integration capabilities with enhanced functionalities. Although static metasurfaces have recently become tunable by altering either the intrinsic electric permittivity of meta-atoms or their immediate vicinity, substantial speed in these changes often struggles without resulting in increased physical bulk. In this work, we introduce an exceptionally thin, tunable metalens capable of adjusting its focal length via optomechanical control under moderate continuous wave intensities. This device delivers focal shifts exceeding 5% rapidly, with a response time on the scale of 10μs.

Telepresence robots (TPRs) function as remotely operated vehicles that facilitate long-distance physical presence and interpersonal interaction. Driven by technological improvements and reduced costs, these devices are increasingly embraced across diverse industries, yet achieving a satisfying user experience remains vital for widespread adoption, specifically addressing not only remote communication but also remote-controlled robot navigation—an often overlooked aspect of TPR operation. This research centers specifically on remote navigation by presenting findings from a comprehensive study that systematically evaluates Quality of Experience (QoE) for real-world Internet-based TPR use. In this setup, participants virtually entered a remote workspace and executed standard TPR tasks such as driving, turning, and parking. By methodically degrading specific visual and control elements of the user's experience through adjustable network variables (including bandwidth, delay, and packet loss), we examined how these impairments are perceived. Our findings demonstrate that users can effectively distinguish between visual and navigational control facets of their interactions and that their sensitivity to degradation in QoE shifts depending on the specific task being performed.

Specifically, if the latency period is shorter than the infection duration, the fraction of afflicted individuals grows exponentially over time to oscillation cycles, potentially accounting for the periodic patterns identified by public health authorities. Furthermore, the model indicates that periodic epidemiological surveillance can misestimate infection trends unless its cycle length perfectly aligns with the infection's characteristic timeframe. The analysis also elaborates on diffusion and relaxation phenomena intrinsic to this framework and their association with infection timelines characteristic parameters, providing further discussion on these processes and their relation.

We introduce oracle-efficient methods to boost adversarial robustness in barely robust learning scenarios. In these cases, learning algorithms produce predictors with robust coverage restricted to just a small subset ($\beta \ll 1$) of the data distribution. Our definition of barely robust learning necessitates guarantees against a broader class of perturbations, and demonstrates this requirement is crucial because weaker conditions fail to ensure robust learning to other degrees, thus establishing the conditions needed for strongly robust learning to be attainable through these means. This confirms distinct but equivalent behaviors between what seem different: strongly and barely robust learning tasks.

This paper introduces a novel learning analytics methodology designed to investigate how educational resources are utilized within MOOCs, specifically targeting course designers as the primary audience seeking to refine their learning materials. Our unique perspective reframes learner dropout not as a metric of failure, but as a valuable indicator used to generate new features for analysis. Supporting this concept is the development of a prototype system, RUAF, tailored to process dataset formats from the FutureLearn platform. In our proof-of-concept study, we apply this tool to interactational data from learners in four distinct MOOCs and validate the accuracy of its outputs by benchmarking against established process mining techniques. Finally, we showcase results that expose distinct resource usage patterns among users and illustrate the practical insights these findings provide for improving curriculum design.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) models have revolutionized the paradigms for addressing vision, speech, and language challenges. Their vast architectures often lead to slow inference and a phenomenon termed "overthinking" in sequence tasks like automatic speech recognition, where predictions generated by final network layers underperform those from earlier ones. Early exit (EE) strategies can address these limitations by enabling dynamic reduction of computations during inference for specific inputs, a concept already common for classification tasks in vision and language yet underutilized in sequence-to-sequence tasks like automatic speech recognition, which typically suffer from degradations in early-layer predictions. Furthermore, performance degrades significantly in asymmetric settings due to the application of speech SSL models on out-of-distribution (OOD) data or the underfitness of earlier layers. In the context, we emphasize that in-domain data also exhibits similar patterns of "overthinking" in speech SSL. We utilize a theoretical framework that quantifies a performance–speed trade-off limit as the basis for new approaches designed to achieve EE with automatic speech recognition, which includes using an adaptation from other areas such as the recent patience scheme.
Furthermore we discuss strategies, each achieving a higher-level accuracy rate than comparable techniques. We provide various technical steps toward optimizing the model, such as proposing (i), an application of a recent patience-derived method to ASR; or second, a brand new early exit design, which performs substantially greater than comparable techniques.

The widespread crisis of the Coronavirus (COVID-19) has negatively impacted both public health and the global economy, characterized by a rapidly rising caseload with no immediate signs of decline. This surge has resulted in critical shortages of testing kits and effective diagnostic models, yet recent evidence suggests chest X-ray radiography offers superior efficacy compared to laboratory testing. Consequently, analyzing chest X-rays serves as an essential tool for the early detection of suspect cases. However, since patient data involves sensitive medical records—potentially exposed during model reconstruction by malicious actors via parameter updates—rigorous protection mechanisms are mandatory. This paper introduces a privacy-preserving Federal Learning framework dedicated to diagnosing COVID-19 using thoracic imagery. First, the study outlines constructing a decentralized learning environment across various healthcare facilities while maintaining data localization at each site. Second, while the research highlights a notable reduction in FedLearning identification accuracy for Non-IID datasets, it proposes specific enhancements: expanding the client pool, increasing parallelism (client fraction), and boosting per-client computation to restore accuracy on such unevenly distributed data. Finally, Differential Privacy Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) is implemented to fortify the privacy of the FL model. Furthermore, practical strategies were developed to ensure the system's overall robustness, thereby balancing security against maintaining high diagnostic accuracy in hospitals where patients may suffer different diseases during an active global crisis.

Innovation significantly propels economic and social progress, much of which is recorded in semi-structured patent data; although traditional methods struggle to quantify this newness and novelty, machine learning provides superior tools to analyze meaning, synthesize contributions, and assess originality. We present the Harvard USPTO Patent Dataset (HUPD), a vast corpus comprising over 4.5 million English-language patent applications submitted to the USPTO from 2004 to 2018. This dataset is exceptionally well-organized, larger than comparable collections by a factor of two to three, and specifically utilizes the inventor's original application texts rather than the finalized granted versions, allowing researchers to study granting decisions based on initial NLP methods for the first time. Uniquely, HUPD integrates abundant structured metadata with the raw filing text, empowering scientists to develop new NLP protocols that account for variations in structured data variables. Demonstrate the research potential inherent to HUPD, we have introduced a fresh NLP challenge—distinguishing between approvals as the central case study utilizing the metadata to explicitly track shifts in underlying concepts—while also validating the data utility alongside for multi-category classification, language model generation, and text summarization in three additional domains of invention subject classifications.

Current trajectory prediction methods typically leverage tracklets to anticipate pedestrian movements using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, yet this study demonstrates that integrating vislet—compact sequences of head pose observations—notably improves these predictions. We present MX-LSTM, a new framework that captures the interaction between tracklets and vislet through joint unconstrained optimization of full covariance matrices via LSTM backpropagation, while simultaneously forecasting future head poses to enhance existing long-term prediction capabilities. By combining these vislet-driven approaches with a head pose estimator and an attentive social pooling mechanism, our model sets a new state-of-the-art on benchmark platforms including Zara01, Zara02, UCY, and TownCentre. The model notably achieves significant performance margins when observing decelerated pedestrians, a challenge where most standard forecasting techniques frequently struggle to deliver accuracy.

While program synthesis in the Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) field is conventionally considered untype-based, we examine the advantages of introducing user-defined types to background knowledge. Building on a Meta-Interpretive Learning (MIL) framework, we demonstrate that employing type constraints effectively narrows the program synthesis hypothesis space. Integrating polymorphic type checking into MIL for logic programming validation is supported by significant theoretical findings and empirical data, which reveal a cubic decrease in both search space magnitude and compilation duration relative to the count of typed predicates employed. Moreover, our method allows for the derivation of polymorphic types across individual inferred clauses and complete generated programs, offering further enhancements by leveraging refinement techniques within ILP to expedite the elimination of irrelevant hypotheses.

The composition of the materials driving relativistic outflows that cause gamma-ray bursts has remained an unresolved question. A primary argument supporting magnetically dominated outflows is notably exemplified by GRB 080916C, where the broadband time-resolved spectra lack an observed photospheric feature. In this study, we conduct a time-resolved analysis of the aforementioned event, validating prior findings of an additional spectral component. Our results demonstrate that this extra component matches the properties of the photosphere within the photospheric layer during the coasting phase of an ultra-relativistic, predominantly baryonic outflow. Therefore, contrary to previous assertions, the necessity of magnetic dominance is invalidated when modeling or identifying this specific event. Furthermore, the observation of high-energy radiation during its initial stage implies the involvement more characteristics of multi-zone emission rather that a one-zone theory.

While 3D point cloud data has gained broad acceptance as a standard format for representing 3D signals, its potential use in estimating the dense correspondence between three-dimensional shapes remains largely unexplored. Additionally, existing few 3D point cloud approaches usually neglect the fundamental, yet widely acknowledged, principle of one-to-one matching. In addressing these gaps, we introduce a novel end-to-end deep learning method that formulates point-based matching as a binary assignment problem, ensuring strict adherence to permutation constraints and the one-to-one requirement. Since traditional algorithms for this assignment problem are non-differentiable and hinder deep learning workflows, we develop a specialized module that first solves for a doubly stochastic (approximate permutation) matrix before mapping it back to an exact permutation. Specifically designed to facilitate seamless backpropagation without disrupting the optimization process via the permutation constraint, our method computes the loss on the optimized permutation while propagating gradients solely through the doubly stochastic variables, enabling effective learning of the assignment. Our flexible framework handles both non-rigid and rigid deformations in 3D point clouds; experimental validation demonstrates that our approach outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art results in 3D dense correspondence estimation.

Evaluated against heterogeneous IoT devices recorded at a real-world smart home router as well as an existing open dataset, results show that IoTAthena successfully defines activity signatures through the provided traffic data and accurately reverts the raw network stream into distinct sequences of IoT activities.

Index theorems connect the metric and gauge fields on a manifold to solutions of the corresponding Dirac equation. In typical distribution networks, the elevated Resistance-to-Reactance (R/X) ratio renders the system's voltage sensitive to power injected by distributed energy resources (DERs). To address voltage violation risks arising from high photovoltaic (PV) penetration in such systems, this study presents a two-stage stochastic optimization approach for determining the optimal positioning and upgrading of PV inverters to enhanced smart inverters featuring Volt-VAr capabilities. This strategy provides guidance for retrofitting existing units for Volt-VAr operation that aligns with operational control constraints. A significant benefit of this planning method is its reliance on local control features independent of external communications, thereby eliminating potential communication outages and latency. The internet increasingly serves as a target for malicious security attacks and intrusions, which can result in network outages, operational malfunctions, or data theft or corruption. Traditional Network Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) function by monitoring traffic to identify malicious or unauthorized activity. However, advanced systems typically attempt to recognize a threat only after inspecting all aspects of the occurring attack, which means damage is often already sustained before the intrusion is halted. In this paper, we introduce a novel, end-to-end framework for detecting intrusions at their earliest possible stage to mitigate damage and avoid unplanned interruptions. Unlike previous approaches that depend on manual feature selection from raw network traffic data, our method employs a deep neural network-based classifier trained in a supervised fashion to automatically extract relevant features from raw inputs. Additionally, we present a new evaluation metric termed "earlines" to quantify the timing of our detection. Validation conducted on the CICIDS2017 benchmark dataset empirically confirms the efficacy of our approach, which achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.803.

Over the last ten years, public discourse has increasingly migrated to social media platforms. This paper introduces a five-stage methodology capable of isolating, classifying, and investigating the hidden argumentation frameworks within online discussions. Focused on tweets concerning the expected ramifications of a "no-deal" Brexit scenario, we first utilize regular expressions (RegEx) targeting verbs linked toCreation, Destruction, and Causation to pull cause-effect claims. Second, we categorize these specific effects through a Structural Topic Model built on unigrams and bigrams. In the subsequent steps, we identify contentious topics and examine partisan disparities in how "in" parties within the debate discuss them using type assignments of covariate effects, before employing a topical correlation network to map the debate's topography and discover cohesive argument clusters. Ultimately, we analyze the temporal evolution of the discourse to deduce lead/follow dynamics between factions. Our methodology proves effective in facilitating a quantitative analysis of rhetoric and tracing the structural organization of controversy over time. Specifically, the Brexit discussion exhibits an assortative argumentation topology defined by faction-based constellations and extreme polarization driven by frames associated with Creation and Destruction. These results underline the value of systemic approaches in exposing the interdependencies between factions and topics in online argumentation.

Deep learning advancements are heavily dependent on access to extensive, accurately labeled datasets. To alleviate this issue and achieve robust performance despite a minimal amount of labeled images, few-shot learning was developed. Despite these benefits, a critical yet often ignored element remains poor image/template selection prior to training, which significantly impacts the final outcome. We introduce the Sample Choosing Policy (SCP) as an innovation tailored specifically for medical landmark detection in a few-shot framework. SCP operates through three components: a) using self-supervised training (to generate a refined model that learns image features from medical scans); b) Key Point Proposal (to detect meaningful visual regions) ; c) Representative Score Estimation (to search and choose the templates most descriptive samples for annotation). SCP has been proven effective via numerous testing procedures using three prominent publicly available datasets. Regarding one-shot detection on both the Cephalometric and HandXray datasets: SCP has significantly diminished mean radial error by a total of 35.65% and lowered it from approximately 3.6mm down to roughly 3.1mm, on average.

The creation and assembly of annotated datasets represent a primary obstacle in machine learning workflows, a challenge intensified by deep learning and other automated feature extraction methods, which generally rely heavily on extensive training data. Weak-supervision methods offer an offset, yet current solutions present significant trade-offs: users must craft comprehensive rule sets (e.g., Snorkel) or, conversely, provide limited labeled data samples for automatic rule discovery (e.g., Snuba, which often requires finding specific patterns in small datasets that perform well). Manual labeling becomes tedious and slow. Additionally, obtaining labeled subdata can be financial burdensome and practically unviable for imbalanced scenarios, wherein an arbitrarily chosen subset often yields too few positive cases due to their scarcity.

Addressing these limitations is the goal of the proposed interactive system, Darwin. This system eases the rule-writing process in weakly-supervised environments for natural language. Starting with a single initial labeling rule and receiving user feedback, Darwin iteratively synthesizing and adapting candidates to address the immediate labeling problem. Scholars discuss how the system, which operates across large-scale corpora exceeding one million sentences, supports any marking function expressible as context–free grammacies (unlike existing algorithms limited to certain expression rules). Further research involves experiments with five real-world datasets indicating the system's effectiveness as being able label words cheaply yet fairly. Specifically, Darwin discovered 40 more positive instances than Snub (when Snub had previously labeled one thousand examples), assuming no prior information.

This research derives critical limits on sensor-based sensorless feedback to enhance rotor angle stability using local frequency or phase data. Analysis of a two-machine power system model reveals an unavoidable tradeoff: improving damping for inter-area oscillations inherently diminishes transient stability margins, independent of the specific control methodology employed. This fundamental restriction occurs because external disturbances triggering inter-area modes cannot be reliably estimated solely from local frequency information. Validation was performed on a modified Kundur four-machine, two-area test system, where active power modulation on a high-voltage direct current (HTDC) link demonstrated these findings. Specifically, utilizing local phase angle measurements for damping control inevitably exacerbates rotor angle deviations following certain load disturbances, potentially causing transient instability in heavily stressed conditions. Consequently, the derived constraints underscore the necessity for wide-area monitoring capabilities in oscillation damping strategies for power systems.

Passivity is a fundamental precondition enabling quantum systems to reach thermodynamic equilibrium and for temperature as a concept to manifest. Despite extensive exploration, the transition from single-shot passivity to a fully pass Gibbs state is understood mathematically but requires deeper intuitive clarity; we address this by recasting quantum passivity in geometric terms, rendering the emergence Gibbs states from passive configurations entirely evident. Clarifying prior findings and extending them to non-equilibrium quantum contexts, our approach assigns every passive state a specific 2D convex shape where the figure's area quantifies the distance of its state from thermal equilibrium. This introduces a unique geometric metric for thermodynamical non-equilibrium, correlated with both ergotropy and $\beta$-thermality (athermality).

In imitation learning, demonstrators serve as the source policy, while imitators aim to mimic that behavior to ensure future events mirror a hypothetical scenario where only the demonstrator acted throughout the interaction. In stochastic environments, errors often compound, leading to drastically divergent outcomes. Previous studies offered rigorous formal guarantees only for settings where both the demonstrator and imitators periodically restart; however, outside this restricted context—where systems run continiously without reset—such formal safety assurances were absent. We tackle this general scenario: the stochastic environment and actor operate without resetting anywhere in the learning cycle (not even for training)—with the learning agent interacting directly with the expert. We introduce a Bayesian learner designed with conservatism by deliberately underestimating all action probabilities and filling remaining probability mass with additional data requests. Our primary finding guarantees an upper bound on the probability of events if those events were deemed unlikely under the expert; because the learner begins ignorant, this bound holds. Simultaneously, as the expert becomes better informed through online learning, interaction queries rapidly decline. Notably, this agent is "safter" because the framework bounds the occurrence of "dangers"—any event deemed hazardous would effectively fail to happen.

We introduce an interactive probing instrument designed to formulate and evaluate "what-if" scenarios for multivariate time series forecasting.
